title: The team of women protecting South Africa's last black rhinos
en: What's up, sunshine? Coy Wire here with your CNN 10 Minutes of News for July 17th, another summer Friday edition catching us up on some of the biggest storylines of the week. If you're wondering about the background, it's because this dude wore this shirt, and I just look like a floating head. So here we are.
Let's start today with a little brain teaser. If you have three, you have three. If you have two, you have two.
But if you have one, you have none. What is it? I'll give you a second. Give up?
Answer is a choice, because if you only have one, it's not a choice.
So thank you for choosing to spend part of your day with us. Now let's get to your news. We're kicking off this with the world's biggest sporting event.

Earlier this week, the World Cup semifinals took place in Dallas. France's Kylian Mbappé and Ousmane Dembele looking to reach a third straight World Cup final facing Spain with 19-year-old sensation Lamine Yamal, who plays like pressure is just another defender to dribble past.
Then in Atlanta, it was defending champs Argentina led by 39-year-old Lionel Messi in what could be his final World Cup, taking on England, looking to lift its first World Cup trophy since 1966.
Now the stage is set. It'll be Spain taking on Argentina on Sunday in New Jersey. One match, 90 minutes, maybe more, and a chance to become the team their nation remembers forever.

Now to a microscopic menace that's having a hugeimpact on cookouts all across the country this summer. It's a single-celled parasite called Cyclospora, wreaking havoc in several states. It causes a condition called cyclosporiasis, which can include weeks of uncomfortable gastrointestinal issues.

While state and federal investigators say they've yet to determine the source behind the surge in cases, Cyclospora commonly passes to humans via raw fruits and vegetables. Our Jacqueline Howard has some tips on what to do to avoid it and what to do if you come down with a serious stomach bug.

Here's what you need to know. In some cases, this illness has been tied to eating fresh produce. And the illness that we're talking about here is called Cyclosporiasis. It's caused by the parasite Cyclospora.

And health officials are investigating cases across several states. In some of those states, Illinois, New York, Pennsylvania, and Texas, cases have been linked to eating fresh produce from Mexican-style restaurants, local chain grocery stores, and catered events. Some examples of produce potentially include cilantro, onions, and cucumbers.

Now there are at least eight additional clusters of cases that are still under investigation in several other states as well. And Cyclosporiasis, it causes intestinal illness. So symptoms include watery diarrhea, in some cases, explosive diarrhea.
And these symptoms can last for weeks. The illness can be treated with antibiotics, but it can be a very miserable illness.

So you want to avoid getting sick in the first place. To do that, avoid food or water that may be contaminated with feces. Experts say that's how this parasite can spread. Also, make sure you thoroughly wash any fresh fruits or vegetables that you have.
If you have firm fruits like melons, scrub them with a brush. And basic hygiene goes a long way. Wash your hands with soap and water, especially before preparing food. Back to you.
All right. On Capitol Hill, lawmakers are rememberinga longtime public servant whose career stretched across decades.

South Carolina Republican Lindsey Graham died last Saturday after suffering an aortic dissection caused by cardiovascular disease, according to the D.C. Medical Examiner. The 71-year-old served in the Senate for 23 years, was a congressman before that. He was an Air Force veteran, also ran for president in 2016.
Senator Graham was also up for reelection, and the filing period for candidates interested in running for the seat begins next Tuesday.
Pop quiz hotshot. A group of rhinos is known as what? A thunder, a crash, a rumble, or a stomp? If you said crash, you rhino-your-stuff.

And if you're wondering where the term originated, just picture a pack of these prodigious pachyderms charging through the brush. Between their massive size and poor eyesight, rhino's not exactly known for their agility.
On the black market, a single rhino horn can fetch tens of thousands of dollars, making the animals dangerously appealing to poachers.

But in South Africa, one remarkable team is fighting back. They're called the Black Mambas, an all-woman group of wildlife rangers protecting wildlife from poaching, not with guns, not with bullets, but with a keen eye and relentless patrols. Garbhajan Hossaini wrote along to see how they get it done.

This is Greater Kruger National Park in South Africa, nearly 5 million acres of wilderness and home to some of the most extraordinary wildlife on the planet, including some of the last black rhinos on earth. There are just over 200 of them left in this park. Protecting them is a group unlike any other. The Black Mambas.
36 strong, battle-hardened, relentless, and unapologetically entirely female. Rhino poaching across South Africa fell 16% last year according to government data.
But inside Kruger, it nearly doubled. Here a black or white rhino is poached on average every 50 hours. Rhinos here are targeted for one reason. Their horn.
The black market is mostly driven by demand in Vietnam and China, where it's used in traditional medicine and as a status symbol, despite the fact that it has no proven medicinal value at all.

To stop this trade, the Mambas patrol nearly 40,000 acres every single day. And they do it completely unarmed. It's an unconventional approach in a world where most anti-poaching units carry weapons. It's not an oversight. It's a philosophy.
Poachers are dangerous. And you all operate unarmed. That seems like a bad idea to me.
Actually, it is a good idea to us because it's been 12 years doing this. None of us has been killed by poachers.
And that's because we constantly get trained. But also we're not threats to the poachers.
So how do you prevent them if they know you don't have guns, if you can't hurt them?
So they know that we're not going to hurt them, then there's no need for them to use their bullets on us as we're not going to respond.
But your presence will still scare them away.
Our presence scares them away because they don't want to be seen. They don't want to be arrested.
So they just want to come inside the reserve, kill the rhino, get the horn and out. And that's why they're always running.
Before the Black Mambas, women were largely shut out of frontline ranger roles in this region. These women didn't just change how this reserve is protected. They opened a door that didn't exist.
So many people didn't believe in us, but we have proved a lot of them wrong.

They learned on us in the reserve. When we do roadblock sometimes in those first years, some of them, they wouldn't even allow us to search them or to touch their car. When now they have elephants are breaking into their house, into their lodges and like things are missing. Now they call the Black Mambas.
Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10, a new twist on summer camp where sparks are flying literally. They're calling it the heavy metal summer experience.

The point is to give teens hands on experience with trades like welding, HVAC repair and electrical work. It started as one camp in Palo Alto, California. It's now expanded to 62 locations in the US and Canada.
When we got hands on with power drills and saws and all kinds of different things, I was really, really excited.
There's historically a stigma with blue collar and construction, and we need to eliminate that.
This actually provides a five year college program through Foothill.
It was free and I was getting paid to work. So it was great.

Organizers say one motivation looking to address a major labor shortage across these industries.It's estimated that there will be a need for two million skilled trades workers in under five years, and they tout that an apprentice can earn a six figure salary by their seventh year.

All right, Sunshine, we have two shout outs today. This first one goes to Mrs. McNeil and Mr. Turway at Northeast Regional Correction Center in Saginaw, Minnesota.Thank you so much for making us a part of your summer and keep up the great work.
Next shout out. This one goes to Mrs. Allard at St. Thomas the Apostle School in West Springfield, Massachusetts.
Thank you for subscribing and commenting on our CNN 10 YouTube channel. Rise up. Hope you have an awesome weekend.
Keep asking great questions. Keep chasing curiosity. And remember, you are more powerful than you know.
See you next Friday. I'm Coy Wire and we are CNN 10.

title: Why an iconic footwear brand is ditching shoes for A.I.
en: What's up, sunshine? I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10, the best 10 minutes in news. Hope you are finding fun ways to spend your summer.
I've just been practicing my ABCs backwards. ZYXWVUTSRQPONMLKJIHGFEDCBA. It's going okay so far.

Today, we have one famous sneaker company lacing up for an AI makeover. And we're going to show you a soccer league proven you don't need superstar salaries to create superstar passion, but first, another nation hits the pause button on social media.
We begin in France, making headlines this week,not just for the Tour de France, but for becoming the first country in the European Union to ban social media for those under the age of 15.

French lawmakers overwhelmingly voted Tuesday in favor of the bill, which was championed by President Emmanuel Macron. He will now sign it into law. Macron pushed lawmakers to move quickly so the new rules could be in place before students head back to school.

This September, the new law will be enforced by France's audio, visual and digital communications regulator are calm. The agency says French teenagers spend an average of nearly 90 minutes every day on Tick Tock alone. The ban is expected to apply to major social media platforms, although exactly how companies will verify users ages is still being worked out.

Some parents say it's a step in the right direction. Others wonder whether it goes far enough. France isn't alone. Of course, Australia made history last year by banning social media for children under 16. The United Kingdom plans similar restrictions next year, while Spain, Greece and Denmark are exploring minimum age requirements of their own.
Next up, imagine your favorite shoe company saying we're done making shoes. Well, if this sounds like it's a setup to a joke, it's not it is real.

Earlier this year, iconic sneaker maker Allbirds stunned customers by announcing it was stepping away from footwear and reinventing itself as an artificial intelligence company called SmartBird. What sounds like an April Fool's prank has become one of the boldest examples yet of businesses betting their futures on AI. Our Claire Duffy spoke to the SmartBird president and CEO about the company's decision to go all in on artificial intelligence.

The company that made these sneakers is dropping Allbirds for AI. News this spring that Allbirds was rebranding as SmartBird sent the company's shares soaring nearly 600%. But it also left some wondering whether it was a joke or a gimmick. New CEO Nadia Carlsten says she's very serious.

There's a lot backing this up. It's the fact that we have a new company now very much dedicated to AI. We have a board that is committed and this is something that I have done before. So I know that it's a market that exists and something that we can deliver.
SmartBird wants to provide computing power for companies to run AI systems, a business that is dominated by giants like Amazon, Google and Microsoft.
AI is so hot right now. This is maybe an unusual way to start an AI company. But it wouldn't be unusual for a company that wants to provide value to choose to be an AI.
It's not the first time a struggling legacy company has made a bold bet on a hyped up new technology. And it doesn't always pan out.
In 2018, film company Kodak announced it was going all in on blockchain and launching its own cryptocurrency. While that news initially sent the company's stock up, the effort quickly fizzled.
Last year, Kodak warned investors it was on the verge of bankruptcy. But SmartBird's Carlsten says she's confident about the opportunity in AI. As for whether she'll miss the shoes.

I actually never owned an Allbirds shoe. People talk about Allbirds being the preferred shoe brand of tech bros. And of course, I am in this space, but I'm one of the few women in the AI infrastructure business. So I'm not a tech bro. And I actually tend to prefer high heels myself.
Pop quiz hotshot.Roughly how long does it take sunlight to reach Earth? Eight minutes, 15 minutes, 27 minutes or 43 minutes?
If you said eight minutes, you are sunsational. Even though the sun is about 93 million miles away, it's light reaches us in just eight minutes and 20 seconds. That's less time than this show.

Summer break is here. That might mean more beach trips, more camping trips. And if your parents or anything like mine, they're probably yelling, put your sunscreen on, son. Or maybe trying to get you to wear one of those sun shirts when you're swimming.

So how much does that stuff really work, though? And just how dangerous is the sun that we need to protect ourselves from it? We are going to turn to our very own CNN medical correspondent Meg Terrell for some answers. Meg, just how dangerous is the sun that we need to protect ourselves from it?

Hi, Coy. Well, the main reason is that the sun produces something called UV rays or ultraviolet light. Now, some of it can be good, helping the body produce vitamin D, but too much can damage the skin cells and potentially lead to skin cancer.
And we definitely want to avoid that. So what are some of the best ways to protect ourselves from the sun?
Well, covering up, wearing a swim shirt, a hat, sunglasses, and of course, sunscreen. There are a couple of different types, chemical and mineral or physical.

And the main difference is the way they provide protection against the sun. Chemical sunscreens usually contain ingredients like avobenzone and octisalate. They work by absorbing the sun's rays and preventing them from damaging the skin.
Mineral or physical sunscreens have ingredients like zinc and titanium dioxide, and they work more like a shield that reflects UV light off the skin.
The main difference is chemical sunscreens take a few minutes to become effective. So be sure to apply early before going out into the sun.

Either way, you want to make sure you get at least SPF 15 and make sure it's broad spectrum. So protecting against both UVA and UVB rays and apply it liberally to any skin that's exposed to the sun. You want to make sure you reapply every two hours that you're outside and after swimming.
And if you're using a spray form, make sure it actually goes where you're intending and not off into the wind.
Okay, sunscreen and a hat. Got it. Now, what if it's cloudy? Then do I have to wear it?
Well, a good rule of thumb is to check the UV index for the day. Any day it's three or higher is a day for sun protection.

Meg Terrell, thank you so much. And how fitting is it that we're talking about sun protection because July is UV awareness month. So as you're having fun this summer, take that extra second or two to put on that sunscreen, your future skin will thank you.
The 2026 World Cup is officially in the books.

Congrats once again to Spain for taking home the trophy. But while soccer's biggest stage has gone dark, the beautiful game is still shining in some unexpected places. In China, a league that began in one of the country's poorest provinces has become a national sensation and fans cannot get enough. Our Mike Valerio has more on how one special league is refreshing reminder that sometimes the purest version of sport isn't played under the brightest lights. It's played for hometown pride.
On the pitch in a remote corner of northern China, the chanting, dancing and thousands of fans hanging on every shot.
This isn't the World Cup. This is Cun Chao China's amateur village Super League.
Right back, Tong Zihao and his teammates are one win away from Cun Chao glory.
But first, he has teeth to fix. Tong, the dentist becomes Tong, the defender.
You could say it's a dream come true. Standing in the spotlight like this, it's not something I normally get the chance to experience.
Like Tong, nearly all the players have day jobs. Professionals are barred, giving amateurs a stage of their own.

That grassroots model reverses the top down path Chinese soccer has pursued for years. Beginning in the 2010s, China's property giants spent billions bringing international stars into the professional league. The spending brought a brief burst of success before China's property boom unraveled, along with bribery and match fixing scandals.
All this despite Chinese leader Xi Jinping himself an avid fan, making soccer a national priority.

So there are no multimillion dollar contracts here. As soon as all these guys are done work, they pack up their things, drive for hours, put on their cleats and come here because of their love of the game.

While Tong and his team step onto the pitch for the final, the entire community gathers at the stadium near festive performances and bustling night markets. But above all, they're here to cheer on their home team. Sun Chao offers what money and mandates struggle to produce, local stars playing for the communities, cheering them on.

Today's story getting a 10 out of 10, a nutty world record that is sure to crack you up. The town of Luverne, Minnesota claims to have more nutcrackers than people, and they've added one giant addition to their roster. The world's tallest nutcracker, Verne the Patriot stands at a jaw dropping 66 feet tall.

That's more than twice the height of the previous record holder in Neuhausen, Germany. And yes, the star spangled superstar has a working jaw. The nutcracker craze was started by 96 year old local legend Betty Mann, who donated her epic collection to the town to help drive tourism.

Nutcrackers aren't just a holiday tradition in Luverne. They're a year round celebration. Every summer, the town hosts nutcracker fest proving they're willing to go to great lengths to crack a smile safe to say Betty and company are crushing it.
All right, rise up. We have two shout outs today. This first one goes to Miss Tara at Lakeside International School in Guanacaste, Costa Rica. Thank you for hanging out with us today and pura vida.
pura vida: Have a great day!

Next up we have Mrs. Gee or Miss Gee for Mrs. Great at the Misericordia School in Chicago, Illinois. Thank you for subscribing and commenting on our YouTube channel and making CNN 10 part of your classroom.
Stay cool. Stay curious. Stay kind.
Make someone smile today. Remember you are more powerful than you know. I'm Coy Wire and we are CNN 10.

title: A Georgia Swamp, a WWII Battlefield and others just earned World Heritage Status
en: What's up, sunshine? I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10, where we give you the what letting you decide what to think. Today, two high stakes meetings at the White House that could shape overseas wars.
A swamp, a mountain, and a World War II battlefield all earning one of the world's highest honors. And BTS, taking a stand against the Grammys, all that and more. Your CNN 10 starts now.

We begin in Washington, D.C., where the Oval Office played host to back-to-back meetings that could influence conflicts stretching from Eastern Europe to the Middle East. On Tuesday, U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky at the White House as Russia continued launching heavy attacks across Ukraine. The two leaders discussed the U.S. giving Ukraine Patriot missile defense systems, which are designed to intercept incoming missiles, as well as the possibility of reviving diplomatic efforts to end the war now in its fourth year.

Later that day, President Trump hosted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for talks on the expanding conflict in the Middle East. The meeting came as Netanyahu campaigns for re-election back home. While relations between the two leaders have appeared more strained in recent months, officials from both sides described the talks as productive.
What do a supersized swamp, Greek gods, and a famous World War II battlefield have in common?

They all just earned one of the world's biggest honors. UNESCO's World Heritage List includes places considered so culturally or naturally important that they're viewed as treasures belonging to all of humanity, not just one country. The designation often brings additional conservation efforts aimed at protecting sites from threats like climate change, pollution, and over-tourism.

This week, the committee announced 25 new additions. That includes the beaches of Normandy, in France. On June 6, 1944, during World War II, better known as D-Day, more than 150,000 Allied troops stormed those shores in the largest seaborne invasion ever, helping begin the liberation of Western Europe from Nazi Germany.

Greece's Mount Olympus also made the list. Ancient Greeks believed it was home to Zeus and the Olympian gods, while today's scientists value it for its extraordinary biodiversity with thousands of plant and animal species. And right here in Georgia, Okefenokee National Wildlife Refuge earned World Heritage status as well.

North America's largest freshwater swamp stretches across roughly 700 square miles, nearly the size of Houston, and provides habitat for black bears, sandhill cranes, and thousands of alligators. The newcomers now join legendary sites like Machu Picchu, Taj Mahal, and Australia's Great Barrier Reef.

One of the most popular bands on Earth is sitting out music's biggest award, K-Pop phenom BTS says it won't submit its music for Grammy consideration after the Recording Academy created a new category recognizing Asian pop music performance.

The group says it believes music should be judged by its artistry, not by language or geography. Some fans argue it would effectively box out Asian artists from the Grammy's biggest awards, like Album of the Year. BTS has previously been nominated for five Grammys, but has not won yet.

This year, the group reunited and released a new album after completing their military service. The CEO of the Grammys told CNN he is disappointed, but said, quote, as a music creator, I understand and respect their decision, unquote. The new Asian pop music performance category will debut at the 2027 Grammy Awards in February.
What do you think? Do categories like these create more opportunities or do they risk separating artists who should compete together? Hit pause and discuss.
Ten-second trivia. Which of these comic publishers was founded first? DC, Marvel, Dark Horse or Image?
If you said DC, you're Superman.
DC was launched as National Allied Publications in 1935, but Marvel wasn't far behind, launching in 1939.

Comic-Con 2026 has officially wrapped and once again San Diego transformed into Superhero Central. Since 1970, Comic-Con has grown from a gathering of a few hundred fans into one of the biggest pop culture events on the planet, attracting artists, actors, filmmakers and fans from around the globe.

This year, legendary cartoonist Jeff Smith, the creator of the beloved Bone series, received one of the comic's highest honors, induction into the Eisner Hall of Fame. We had the chance to catch up with him to hear how a love of drawing at a very young age changed his life forever.
Between like five and nine was when I really started to understand to get into comics.

The art form, the pictures and the word balloons and how the pacing as you went from panel to panel, how it became real, how it would come alive. I was fascinated by that. Of course, the characters had a lot to do with it too.
I knew that Charles Schulz created Snoopy. I knew that Mickey Mouse was made up by Walt Disney. He was on television every Sunday night.
And I wanted to make up a character because I just love cartoons. I don't know why cartoons spoke to me, but they did. They look to me kind of the way dreams look to me.

All the comics that I really loved were written and drawn by the same person. It just didn't occur to me that I would do it any other way, right? The first character I really kind of like started drawing more than once was this little guy called Fone Bone. His name was Fone Bone.

This is what he looked like the first time I drew him. Then he had his cranky cousin who was a phony Fone Bone. And then the Smiley Bone was kind of like a cross between Goofy and Ed Norton on the honeymooners.

I was part of a generation that really wanted to do our own characters and tell our own stories and be more like authors than just a penciler. This is a golden age happening and it's kind of underground, but it's open. They're self-publishers. They're smaller boutique publishers. This is an opportunity. This is somewhere I can do the comic exactly as I want it.
I'm just taking the risk myself. And if it doesn't work, it's no big deal. I'll try.
Every two months I put out a new chapter as like a 24 page comic book, Black and White. Bone and the comic book world have pretty high numbers. I was within like 5,000 copies a month of back.
No books were like that. You know, we did not have like all ages books in the 90s. It was really like these comics are aimed at teens and older. And when Bone comes out, it's like a revelation.
The results spoke for themselves. Bone wasn't just a hit comic. It was a business.
It took 12 years and it grew not only in story, but in readership. I mean, I was really getting to know a lot of people and people loved it. I was lightning in a bottle. Everything came together.
Stores got behind it, which was very deliberate. Like Jeff Smith did a lot of work to make that happen. It wasn't an accident. He put together a business plan to self-publish that book.

So now you've got one more hero self-publisher who's talking about his experience doing that. Now that's information I can apply to my own practice. And I have a lot of admiration for Jeff Smith and what he's done.

You spend so much time with that story. I mean, from your conception to outlines, thumbnails, sketches, pencils, tight pencils, inking, coloring, lettering. You live with this story and if you don't love it or understand how much time it's hard.
But the path to success is rarely easy and far from a straight line. At points, Jeff seemed ready to call it quits until he received some encouragement from an unlikely place.

What saved me was the librarians. We didn't know it, but the libraries had been starting to stock there. And they noticed the kids were checking them out. The librarians started calling Scholastic and said, you've got to publish this book.

So Scholastic called us. And we've been approached by publishers before, but they didn't know what to do with it. But Scholastic says we do know what to do with it. We're going to publish it as a children's book and we're going to put it on the shelves right next to Harry Potter.
But behind every great creator, there's a partner helping bring these characters to life. And none of this would be possible without Jeff's longtime partner, Vijaya.

She's been not only my best friend and my partner, but she's also been one of the people who mostly encouraged me to do this. She handles all the business, the agents, the lawyers. To do something this difficult and personal, you need to have somebody on your side.
I don't think there was a chance I could have succeeded on this level had she not been fully vested.

Despite selling more than 10 million books in dozens of countries worldwide, Jeff says he's not done. He's continuing to work on new projects, but says it never gets old to hear that his first drawings are earning new fans every day.
She actually drew this. Isn't that amazing?

The part that's kind of hard for me to take in sometimes is that this book, when they were a kid, had a real effect on it. And it reminds me of when I was that age and I was reading Peanuts and Uncle Scrooge comics, the effect that that had on me.
So it's really wonderful to take in and oh, gosh, it's really a good feeling.
Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10, a really awesome tradition at one of the NFL's oldest stadiums. Some NFL players drive luxury cars to work.

Green Bay Packers players, sometimes they ride bikes borrowed from kids. The Packers opened their training camp with one of the league's most fun traditions, the dream drive. Every summer, young fans line up outside Lambeau Field hoping a player chooses their bike for a ride to practice.

I got to do this when I played for the Buffalo Bills and we had some crossover practices there. It was awesome. From Lambeau to the practice field, sometimes the shortest ride can create memories that last a lifetime.
And get this, they've been doing it for more than 60 years dating back to legendary coach Vince Lombardi. Now that is how you roll to the football season.
All right, before we go, we have a shout out to Mr. Johnson and all of our warriors at Woods Bend Youth Development Center in West Liberty, Kentucky rise up.
And we're also showing some appreciation to Mr. Lee at P25R in Staten Island, New York. Thank you for hanging out with us this summer. You rock.
Two more Summer Friday episodes before we get back to our Monday through Friday jam on August 17th.
Wherever life takes you, be curious, be kind and remember you are more powerful than you know. I'm Coy Wire and we are CNN 10.

title: How an insect-eating plant is proving Charles Darwin right 150 years later
en: What's up, sunshine? This is CNN 10. And today we have fire season rewriting record books. Why America just hit the brakes on foreign made robots and a cyclist taking the ultimate NFL road trip with nothing but two wheels and a whole lot of grit.

I'm Coy Wire. And we begin today with the Pacific Northwest where destructive wildfires are wreaking havoc across Washington and Oregon, as the states endure their worst fire season in more than 30 years. In Washington's Spokane County, a trio of fires has consumed more than 10,000 acres so far with zero percent containment since they started over the weekend.
The fires have forced the evacuation of nearly 65,000 in Spokane area alone, and more than 700 structures have been destroyed.

This all happened in a matter of hours. In other words, individuals woke up in their homes Saturday morning. In a matter of hours, their homes and neighborhoods were just wiped out. This happened very, very quickly.
No injuries or deaths have been confirmed as of this taping, but officials said that the scale of the fires means it will take time to fully evaluate.

Law enforcement says a man has been arrested on an arson charge in connection with one of those, and fire officials are still investigating the cause of the other blazes. The Pacific Northwest isn't the only region feeling the impact from wildfires. More than 27,000 firefighters across the country are battling at least 100 uncontained fires as of this taping, and that was just this week alone.
Wildfires have scorched at least 5.3 million acres across the country so far this year, already surpassing last year's total for the entire year.

We've shown you videos of robot dogs, humanoid robots. Well, now importing those will be banned in the U.S. The U.S. Federal Communications Commission, or FCC, says that importing advanced robotics from certain foreign countries poses an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. Our Mike Valerio will tell us more.
You want to bring a robot like this from China into the United States? Well, forget it. New foreign robots are now banned.

The Federal Communications Commission in Washington just ruled advanced robotic devices produced in foreign countries, quote, pose an unacceptable risk to the national security of the United States. The ban only applies to new imports, not any devices already stateside.
This comes after robots from Chinese companies like Unitree have wowed millions on social media, becoming more familiar to Americans, and even taking the stage on America's Got Talent.
So the U.S. government now says that relying on foreign produced advanced robotic devices presents unacceptable supply chain and cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

Gesundes say advanced robotic devices collect data that could be leveraged by malign actors to surveil Americans, enhance the capabilities of foreign intelligence services, or to remotely commandeer the robots.
90% of the world's humanoid robots are made in China, with more than 140 companies competing in a crowded and quickly expanding market.

Robotics companies and China's Ministry of Commerce for now are not publicly reacting. The move is another potential point of friction as the U.S. and China try to stabilize ties. The FCC says it's possible to avoid the ban if a company applies for an exception, proving the product does not pose a risk and that's signed off by the Pentagon.
This imports ban mirrors other U.S. prohibitions of Chinese tech, like communications equipment from Huawei and Chinese EVs kept out of the U.S. market.
Now to a story about the impact that space junk is having on the moon. And by impact, I mean literally.

A piece of SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket slammed into the moon earlier this week at nearly seven times the speed of sound. The rocket launched about 18 months ago, and its upper stage was intentionally left drifting through space after completing its mission. Normally, leftover rocket parts eventually fall back to Earth and burn up as they enter our atmosphere.
Not this one. Officials say it blasted a crater roughly the size of a Major League Baseball infield. No one could actually see it happen with the naked eye.
Instead, astronomers used a special telescope to see glowing plumes of lithium and sodium gas being kicked into space, almost like the moon briefly left behind its own cosmic fingerprint.
Pop quiz, hot shot. Which U.S. state is home to the only native population of Venus flytraps?
Florida, Hawaii, North Carolina, or California?
If you said North Carolina, you so fly.
Venus flytraps only thrive in bogs and wetlands. In the wild, nearly all of them grow within a tight 70 to 100 mile radius around Wilmington, North Carolina.
More than 150 years after evolutionary scientist Charles Darwin made a bold prediction, science just proved him right.

Darwin believed certain carnivorous plants like Venus flytraps didn't just trap insects, they actually digested them. Back then, he didn't have the technology to prove it. Now, scientists in China use modern genetic and chemical testing on a plant called the saxifraga and confirm that those sticky little plants really do absorb nutrients like nitrogen from the bugs they catch.

Darwin also believed carnivorous plants evolved because they grew in nutrient-poor soil. Turns out he nailed that too. Carnivorous plants still get most of their energy via photosynthesis, just like other plants.

NFL players spend months preparing for a season, one fan is spending 10,000 miles getting ready for week one. 22-year-old ultra-endurance cyclist Bond Almand is currently on a 10,000 mile quest to visit all 30 stadiums by bike ahead of the league's kickoff in Seattle next month. That's roughly the distance from New York to Tokyo and halfway back.

One of our fearless CNN 10 teammates, Brendan, caught up with Bond outside of Atlanta's Mercedes-Benz Stadium to hear how the trip is going and see what motivates him to push himself to the limit in pursuit of greatness.
Most mornings when I wake up, I do not want to get on the bike, I'll be honest. And after a couple hours of riding, I've warmed up, I feel good, I'm loving it.
The bike can take me anywhere, it's a great way to explore.
This is Bond Almand, a one-of-a-kind ultra endurance cyclist who's taking his sport to the next level, one pedal at a time. At just 22 years old, he already has five world records.

In 2024, he shattered the record for fastest north-south Pan-American bike crossing, completing all 14,000 miles from Alaska to Argentina in just 75 days, all of this while balancing his studies at Dartmouth College. Now, the recent grad is spending his summer chasing a new goal, crisscrossing the country on a quest to visit all 30 NFL stadiums. The epic odyssey is the brainchild of Extreme Networks, who pitched the idea to Bond earlier this summer, and even he couldn't believe it.

He originally came to me with the idea, and I was like, that's a great idea, but yeah, there's no way that ever happens. And then he called me a week later and was like, okay, we're all set. Bond set out from Miami on July 7th, carrying a special NFL game ball destined for the league's kickoff game in Seattle on September 9th.

The scenic, and I mean scenic route, is giving him a view of the country that few people ever get to see. But the trip is anything but a leisure ride. Bond is averaging up to 200 miles per day, sometimes climbing as much as 20,000 feet. That's like summiting Mount Kilimanjaro, and mileage like that takes a physical and mental toll.
summit [ˈsʌmɪt] v. to climb to the summit of (a mountain).

The cumulative fatigue every single day, that stress in your body, it's hard to understate. Obviously, I'm one person, but there's like a side of me that wants you to stop and rest. Those two sides have to make peace.
His biggest challenge so far, not the hills, the heat. Bond is losing gallons of sweat every day, so he's found some unique ways to stay hydrated.
I take a lot of table salt and just pour it straight into my water bottle. You can kind of see the salt on your skin, that's all that sodium you're losing. My favorite drink hack is coffee creamer.
If you get a bottle of coffee creamer like this, it has several thousand calories in it.
From serene back roads to bustling city centers, Bond is documenting the entire trip on social media, hoping it'll help raise awareness for other cyclists.
I've been hit by a couple cars before and that really rattles me.

It's always in the back of the mind on the bike and it's part of why I love biking and sharing my story is to kind of get people more familiarized with biking. And if a couple of drivers can see my videos and be excited about biking, maybe give the next biker a little bit more space when they pass, then that's a huge win.
By the time Bond rolls into Lumen Field on September 9th, he'll have clocked more than 10,000 miles, about the same amount most people put on their cars in a year.
And on a trip this big, sometimes the biggest challenge isn't the terrain, it's staying motivated.
One thing that I've suffered with a bit is burnout. I do love my bike and it brings me a lot of joy, but there are days when it just doesn't.
So having that like higher purpose, like what is the goal of riding, why am I doing this, is always important.
His advice for the next generations of endurance cyclists looking to make their own marks?

Believe in yourself more than anything. I was always told from a young age, like do whatever you love, follow your dreams. I think that's 100% true, but it's more complicated than that. I think it's do what you love, but have intention, have some idea of where you want it to take you.
For Bond, that somewhere is chasing the horizon one mile at a time.
Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10, who let the dogs out?

Dozens of four-legged surfers took on some radical waves in Northern California at the 10th annual World Dog Surfing Championship this week. Spectators flocked to the beach and judges scored the pups on how long they could stay on their board, wave size, and confidence.

Surfing is amazing anyways, right, because you're you're community with nature, it's you've got the solitude, you got the Indian, you got the excitement, and then you mix in your best friend because then you're working together as a team to accomplish something.
The contest was cut short because of some rough waves before the final surf off, but that just means they're all winners in our hearts.
All right superstars, we're sending some love today. First, we're going to reach Columbus in Indiana. Thank you for your kind letters. We are so glad you spent part of your summer with us.
And this next shout out goes to Coach Bradley at White House Heritage High School in Tennessee. Rise up. Thank you for commenting and subscribing to our CNN 10 YouTube channel.
Go out, make someone smile, make someone laugh this weekend.
Remember, you are more powerful than you know. I'm Coy Wire and we are CNN 10.

title: The Sun, Moon and Earth Align: Stunning views of the total Solar Eclipse
en: Hello, and happy Friday, Fri-yay. Welcome to our last summer edition of CNN 10 before we start our usual slate of Monday through Friday shows kicking off after the weekend. Now, before we dive into our weekend, we have some of the top news stories from this past weekend.

We will start with the heartbreaking story still developing in Colombia.The South American nation has been devastated by a 7.4 magnitude earthquake, the strongest to hit Colombia in a decade. The quake struck Monday in the western region, sending shockwaves through cities across the country and prompting the government to declare a national disaster.

As of this taping, more than 200 people have been killed, hundreds more injured, a number that's expected to rise as rescue crews continue to work around the clock. Our Reid Binyan has a look at the race to find survivors and how the world is reacting.

Colombia's president on Tuesday touring areas devastated by the massive earthquake that rocked the country Monday, the government declaring a national disaster as the nation's army deploys forces to the most gravely devastated areas.

Some areas hard to reach, including near the quake's epicenter, have yet to receive help, according to one indigenous leader. A United Nations official says distribution of food is critical in the coming days. World leaders are offering assistance, and so are aid groups.
We've already deployed a team. They're already on the ground. The devastation is vast, and it covers a large geographical area.
Volunteers in the U.S. also doing what they can to help. Just trying to help out, you know, whoever might need it.
Those relief efforts coming amid ongoing rescue efforts, emergency responders racing to find people still buried under the rubble.

Volunteers aiding in the daunting task of locating survivors. Video shows the moment an infant was pulled from the wreckage of an apartment building. One of the rescuers said he and several other civilians helped save the child after he heard someone under the rubble calling for help.

The assistance from volunteers coming as first responders need all the help they can get amid the massive rescue effort. Crews also utilizing specialized search and rescue dogs that Colombian police say are playing a key role.
Now to Denmark, where the government is taking an old school approachto trying to curb a next gen problem in the classroom, AI cheating.
High school students will be required to verbally defend their written assignments and any exams written at home as part of emergency measures aimed at combating the trend.

The rules take effect immediately and apply to students in upper secondary education, which typically begins around age 16. The country's Ministry of Education is also calling on high schools to use tools to monitor student screens during exams, as well as firewalls to filter the content they can access during exams and in class.
They're also encouraging schools to get students to complete more assignments in school under controlled environments to make supervision easier.
Pop quiz, hot shot. Which part of the moon's shadow produces a total solar eclipse, penumbra, umbra, corona or terminator?
Go ahead and moonwalk if you said umbra.
The moon's orbit is tilted relative to Earth's orbit around the sun, so in order for a total solar eclipse to occur, all three must be perfectly aligned.
The celestial sky put on quite a show this past week. A total solar eclipse crossed over Iceland, Greenland, Spain and Russia.
For about two minutes, the moon lined up perfectly with the sun, plunging several countries into darkness.
A glowing white halo of light called the corona emerged around the dark disk of the moon. Folks who saw it were feeling all sorts of emotions.
It was fantastic. Really touching, something that I have never seen before. It went completely dark and suddenly the day came again.
I felt goosebumps because it just makes us think about, I don't know, the shortness of life and how time can be different.

And in a rare alignment on Thursday morning, did you catch any of this? The northern hemisphere got a dazzling look at the Perseid meteor shower. Every August, Earth passes through debris left behind by Comet Swift-Tuttle.

NASA says there were excellent viewing conditions because the peak of the shower coincided with a moonless new moon, allowing stargazers to spot 50 to 100 meteors per hour. NASA says the Perseids are the very best meteor showers to observe from Earth.

This next story comes with a lesson. Do not mess with Harry Potter superfans. The Greenlink interconnector is one of Europe's most important energy projects. It's an undersea cable that's designed to connect the electricity grids between Ireland and Wales at a price of more than half a billion dollars.
But it was originally planned to slice right through a Harry Potter filming location, one that has become somewhat of a sacred spot for Potter fans. Our Ivana Skotola is here with what happened next.
Harry Potter fans managed to get an electricity project rerouted, all to protect Dobby's grave.

The grave is actually a memorial for the fictional character on a beach in Wales where Dobby's death scene was filmed. It's a popular tourist spot where fans leave stones, and some travel across the world to visit. The Greenlink interconnector carries electricity between Britain and Ireland through cables going under the Irish Sea.

During the project's development, its planned route was set to go through the fan-made memorial to Dobby the Elf. That's before fans caught wind of the plan, former project manager Simon Ludlam said in a podcast. He said they received hundreds of calls protesting the route after the plans were revealed.

So they ultimately changed the planned route to avoid the grave. It's actually not the first time the memorial has been saved. In 2022, the National Trust considered removing it or relocating it because of the environmental impact it was having on the beach.
In the end, they decided that it could stay open as long as visitors stopped leaving socks and other items that could harm the environment.

Now to a story that is proof that people are never too young to dream big, and it's never too late to make those dreams a reality. When Tahira Reid-Smith was in third grade, she drew a picture of something she always wished she could have, an automated double-Dutch jump rope machine.
Now four decades later, she's an engineer, and she has turned her childhood dream into a rope-spinning reality. I'll skip the puns and let our Scout Richards jump right in for more.
This third-grade drawing became a real invention.
This was in 1986, and all I remember the assignment was to draw a picture of something you wish you could have. And I was an only child at the time. I loved jumping double-dutch.

Now an engineering professor, Reid-Smith turned her childhood idea into a real automated double-dutch machine prototype that turns the rope for you. And she even reunited with her third-grade teacher in the Bronx to show her what became of that assignment.
I was really emotional about it this morning. There's a real teacher that I had that was part of that memory.
Tahira has certainly shown me that anything is possible. And if you have an idea in mind, don't give up on your dream. Go up a little faster.
Members of Chicago's 40-plus double-dutch club got to give the machine a whirl.
If you have a turning machine, then anybody can jump. And it's even something that can help people learn how to jump.
Now, Reid-Smith hopes to bring her invention, aptly called Jump Dreams, into production.
All right, this week's story, getting a 10 out of 10 is you.

The 10th of the month was Monday, so that means we are highlighting some of our viewers' top moments of 2026 so far. A lot of international submissions this month, so let's kick it off in China, where Wei Ling just passed her national postgraduate entrance exam and she received an offer from her dream university. She says, It is my proudest yes-I-did-it moment of the whole year. We are so happy for you and love seeing your two furry fans celebrating with you. It is purr-fect. Congratulations, Gong Xi!

Our next submission comes from Romania, where Bucharest Christian Academy celebrated their diverse student body with a culture festival. Mr. Maynard says their school hosts students and teachers from 11 different countries and everyone was able to share their favorite songs, dance, and most importantly, food. Rise up!

Finally, let's head to Dagsboro, Delaware, here in the United States. Mrs. Sensman shared these photos of the Indian River School Unified Basketball Team, which represented the state of Delaware in this year's Special Olympics.

After a hard-fought tournament, these Olympians brought home silver medals, and their state could not be more proud. Neither can we. Way to go, and thank you for sharing such a momentous accomplishment with us.

That's all for this month's 10 out of 10. If you want to be featured in our September 10th highlights, tell us something good. Send us your dubs, your victories, your milestones, and achievements to CNN10 @ CNN.com. Go make it an awesome weekend, my friends, and starting Monday, we will be back with you every day of the workweek.
Can't wait. I'm Coy Wire, and we are CNN 10.

title: Hurricane Lala: Floods, power outages overwhelm Hawaii's Big Island
en: Hello, and welcome to the show. New season, new stories, new moments that could change the world and maybe even change us. I'm Coy Wire.

This is CNN 10, 10 minutes of going places, meeting people, asking questions, and getting smarter together. No shout in the news, no opinion, no slant. I simply tell you the what, letting you decide what to think.
The world moves fast, but we've got the best 10 minutes in news to keep up. CNN 10 is back. We begin today with Mother Nature reminding us who's boss.

Several significant earth science stories across the globe, starting in Hawaii, where Hurricane Lala battered the islands over the weekend, its eyewall brushing Hawaii's big islands Saturday as the Category 1 storm moved west. A hurricane does not have to make landfall to cause major damage. Lala didn't, but its impact was felt across the state.

Videos obtained by CNN show a surreal scene where torrential rainfall and sustained 80 mile per hour winds left more than 130,000 customers without power. That's about 70% of the big island. It's been really surreal and kind of unreal that we're getting like Lala like right now.
And it said like in three decades we haven't got one like this big.
Hawaii's governor announced at least one person had been killed in a storm related car accident. Emergency crews are working around the clock to restore power and rescue stranded residents.

Lala was downgraded to a tropical storm Sunday as it continued northwest across the rest of the state, dumping more than two to three feet of rain in some areas in less than 24 hours. Tropical storms typically hit cooler ocean temperatures as they approach Hawaii, but Lala remained over warmer waters due to an ongoing maritime heat wave in the Pacific thanks to the developing Super El Nino.
Now to Indonesia, where rescuers are racing the clock to search for survivors following a series of severe earthquakes.

Officials say a 7.7 magnitude quake struck off the coast of Flores Island, home to roughly two million people and the popular tourist hotspot Bali, around 6 a.m. local time Saturday morning. Just hours after the first earthquake, another 6.9 magnitude quake rattled northern Sumatra, followed later by a third 5.7 magnitude quake roughly 600 miles to the north. Flores experienced nearly 1,000 aftershocks following the initial quake.
Roughly 1,300 homes across the island were severely damaged, forcing many residents to flee with just the clothes on their backs.
At the moment we don't dare go home just yet because the situation isn't stable. We still worry that there might be more tremors coming.

As of this taping, at least 50 people have been killed and scores more have been injured. Let's get smarter. Now, we begin today in the Democratic Republic of Congo, where an Ebola outbreak has crossed a grim milestone. It is officially the deadliest Ebola outbreak in the country's history.

More than 2,300 people have died. Nearly 5,000 cases have been confirmed, surpassing the death toll from Congo's devastating 2018 to 2020 outbreak. This outbreak is being driven by the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, a rare form of the virus which there is no currently approved vaccine or proven treatment for.

Its fatality ratio is nearly one in every two cases. Clinical trials are underway for a strain-specific vaccine, as well as two antiviral therapies. The outbreak was officially declared in May, but officials believe it may have started as early as February.

Ebola spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids of infected people, and can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea, and in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. Much of the outbreak is occurring in areas already dealing with weak health care systems, community resistance, and political instability.

But weather forecasters are hopeful that the rest of the Atlantic hurricane season, which ends in November, will remain quieter than normal. One reason? Something happening thousands of miles away in the Pacific Ocean, El Nino.

It occurs when waters in the central and eastern tropical Pacific become unusually warm. And while the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, or NOAA, says that there's a strong chance this Super El Nino will become the strongest on record, aka lots of rain, that could mean fewer hurricanes. Our meteorologist Derek Van Dam is here to explain.

Strong El Ninos, like the one that's building right now, have an outsized influence on the Atlantic hurricane season, reducing both the number and the strength of tropical systems. Now El Nino isn't just about the warmer waters here in the Pacific. It's also a change in global circulation patterns.

These altered patterns shift sinking air across the tropical Atlantic, stabilizing the atmosphere, reducing thunderstorm development that's needed to create a hurricane. Additionally, these circulation changes, they help displace the jet stream across the tropical Atlantic. These strong upper-level winds create wind shear, which is a hostile environment for tropical development and can deliver a death blow to an emerging hurricane.

In the early stages of a tropical storm's life, it needs a calm environment at all levels of the atmosphere to grow. When wind shear is introduced, it disrupts this vertical alignment, making it harder for thunderstorms to organize into a tropical system and get stronger. Now think of a hurricane as a spinning top.

Wind shear would be like pushing this top and altering its spin. This is particularly disruptive when the top is spinning slowly, just like the early formative stages of a tropical system. With more wind shear around, it's harder for budding hurricanes to get over that hump.

Now while wind shear and sinking air can put a big dent in tropical activity throughout the Atlantic, it doesn't eliminate it altogether. Previous El Nino seasons, like the destruction brought on by Hurricane Andrew in 1992, have proven that it only takes one landfall to make this a catastrophic season. So be hurricane ready this year by downloading the all-new CNN weather app.

From storms influenced by the ocean to storms literally made by fire, and scientists are calling in a Cold War legend to help understand them. NASA is using a modified version of a U-2 spy plane to study how wildfires help generate storms. The U-2, nicknamed the Dragon Lady, is capable of flying at extreme altitudes of up to 80,000 feet, more than twice as high as a typical commercial flight.

It served as a crucial eye in the sky for the United States during the Cold War, and has played a pivotal role in aerial surveillance ever since. This version, dubbed the ER-2, is like a flying laboratory. Instead of spying on adversaries, though, it's spying on fire.

Scientists are getting a bird's eye view of pyrocumulonimbus clouds, or fire clouds, as they form. They're some of Earth's least understood weather phenomena. A wildfire can become so hot that it forces massive amounts of heated air, smoke, and moisture upward, and essentially builds its own thunderstorm.

These fire clouds can produce lightning, strong winds, and in some cases, fire tornadoes. Scientists hope that these missions will allow them to better understand and possibly predict these erratic storms in the future.

On August 19th, 1960, two canine cosmonauts named Belka and Strelka blasted off aboard the Soviet spacecraft Sputnik V, becoming the first dogs to orbit Earth and make it home alive.

And they weren't flying solo. Along for the ride, a rabbit, rats, dozens of mice, and assorted plants and fungi, basically Noah's Ark space edition. They orbited the Earth 17 times, spending more than a day in space.

The pups followed Laika, a Soviet dog who became the first living creature to be sent into space in 1957, but sadly did not survive. Belka and Strelka, Russian for squirrel and little arrow, became instant folk heroes back home, and threw the US-Soviet space race into overdrive. Just nine months later, Russia's Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space.

Less than a decade later, in 1969, the US landed on the moon as part of the Apollo 11 mission. So before humans took one giant leap, a couple of very good girls took some pretty important first steps.

This trial that kicked off in federal court in Oakland is part of a case that was brought by 29 state attorneys general.

title: How an AI chatbot is helping this blind man 'see' for the first time
en: Hello and welcome to the show. I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10 and I hope you're having an awesome Friday Eve.

Mine got off to a rough start. My daughter asked, can I have a bookmark? Five years old and she still doesn't know my name is Coy. Let's get to your news for Thursday, August 20th, starting with some unsettling news.
We've already seen more foodborne illness outbreaks in the United States this summer than in any of the previous five summers. We are on pace for a record. Experts say there are several reasons why.

Extreme summer heat can create conditions where some bacteria multiply faster, especially when food isn't kept at safe temperatures, and some pathogens are particularly tough to track down. Pathogens are things like bacteria, viruses, and parasites, and they're capable of causing disease. Funding cuts at the state, federal, and local levels have also made it harder to determine where these outbreaks start.

Speaking of outbreaks, a CNN investigation into one of the biggest companies tied to this summer's cyclospora outbreak, Taylor Farms, is shedding light on how they've handled similar situations in the past and what it could mean for food safety going forward. Our Kyung Law has more.
This is the headquarters for Taylor Farms.
This is private property. Okay. Taylor Farms won't talk to us on camera today.

We'd already asked for an interview and had not heard back. This is the company, the FDA linked to the historic cyclospora outbreak, 6,600 hospitalized and two dead. Here's what we want to ask the company.

The government traced at least five different outbreaks directly to Taylor Farms in the past 13 years, and a CNN review finds time after time the company turned to a similar playbook, deflecting blame. How?

By relying on negative test results to imply that Taylor Farms products are not responsible, even though investigators mainly find the source of outbreaks by figuring out what and where people who got sick ate.
It's deja vu all over again. I sort of feel like we're on a repeat record.

This month, Taylor Farms said, according to the FDA, there are no confirmed positive sample results for product testing for cyclospora as of August 5th, 2026. We are confident in our food and food safety systems.

Let's rewind through the known outbreaks linked to Taylor Farms. 2013, eerily similar cyclospora cases connected to Taylor Farms salad. CEO Bruce Taylor said at the time, all our tests have been negative and we have no evidence of cyclospora in our product.

2015, a multi-state E. coli outbreak. Taylor's public response, the tests were preliminary findings and it looks like a false alarm. The FDA later said a product with Taylor Farms produce was the likely source.
2024, another E. coli outbreak traced to onions distributed by Taylor Farms. The company said it found no traces of the bacteria. All Taylor Farms products in the market today are safe to consume.
I think they have played a little bit fast and loose with the facts.

Food safety attorney Bill Marler has sued Taylor Farms a dozen times in multiple outbreaks representing more than 100 clients. He says the company implies its food may not be to blame by telling the public their testing found no trace of the microbes.
But Marler says that doesn't prove anything.

Taylor Farms is using those negative results to muddy the water. The scientists at Taylor Farms know better that the products that get tested are not the products that people consume. And I always say this and it sounds like I'm making a joke, but people eat the evidence.
About half of America's domestic lettuce is grown here in the Salinas Valley in central California. It's also where Taylor Farms is headquartered.
But the focus of this cyclospora outbreak is in central Mexico at the Taylor Farms facility there. The same plant linked to another cyclospora outbreak in 2013.
It's the same facility. They're drawing iceberg lettuce in from the same area and expecting a different result.
Taylor Farms tells CNN it invests more than $200 million a year in food safety. The problem is that nothing can kill cyclospora on fresh vegetables without cooking.

Now to Colombia where communities are still reeling after last week's devastating 7.4 magnitude earthquake. As the nation begins the process of rebuilding, one of Colombia's most famous daughters is coming home to help. Shakira, the global superstar, returned this week to visit one of the hardest hit areas, the Choco Earthquake Zone.

The four-time Grammy winner has inspired crowds on the biggest stages and now she's trying to inspire something even more powerful, hope. Shakira is helping rebuild 11 local schools in partnership with the Howard G. Buffett Foundation.

We are living through one of the worst tragedies Colombia has ever experienced, but we are united and we are going to fight and we are not going to stop until every child returns to school, until every child can regain a sense of normality, return to their life, to their friends.

This is about more than just bricks and walls. It's about rebuilding routines, community, and a sense that tomorrow might be better than today. More than 280 people were killed and thousands more were injured in last week's quake.

Now to Hong Kong, where artificial intelligence is helping a blind man navigate the world around him like never before. Chung Chi-Ming has been blind since birth, but now using a wearable AI device, he's able to explore and even go shopping in his city all by himself for the very first time. Check it out.
This small device is transforming how 40-year-old Chung Chi-Ming navigates his city. It uses generative AI to detect his surroundings, translating into an audible format.
I'm completely blind, totally blind since birth.
Through AI technology, I can understand the world. Yeah, correct.
Lamia Suraya Raman co-developed the device, called Seeker AI, to be hyperlocal.

Generative AI, or these chatbots, were built for people like you and me, sighted individuals. But what visual-impaired people need is another added layer of information. We've built our own database of information that any visual-impaired person can tap into and navigate.

That extra layer of detail on everyday life is what sets Seeker AI apart. While volunteering during COVID, Lamia realized the elderly and visually impaired people she met weren't using other assistive tech available on the market.
By pressing one button, Ming can get details like expiry dates, nutritional value, or price in up to 12 different languages.
If my friends, my family are not available, this technology is a very good kind of thing to help me to do things independently.
Pop quiz, hot shot.Which species is believed to be the first domesticated by humans?
Horses, sheep, dogs, or birds?
If you said dogs, bow wow wow, yippee yo yippee yay, you've unleashed the right answer.
Scientific evidence suggests domesticated canines were living alongside humans at least 14,000 years ago. Man's best friend for thousands of years.
According to new research from the University of Vienna, Dogs are pretty good at reading the room.

They can detect when we're happy, when we're sad, even scared. Researchers scanned the brains of eight dogs while showing them images of strangers, displaying emotions from happiness to sadness, anger, even fear. When the dogs saw happy human faces, researchers detected increased activity in brain regions associated with higher-level processing and reward.

They responded differently to negative emotions, but their brains still showed distinct patterns of activity. So they may not know why we're having a rough day, but scientists suggest they may know something is up.
Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10, Hollywood's most famous sidewalk just added a groundbreaking new star.

Hailing from Benin, music icon Angelique Kidjo made history this week, becoming the first Black African performer to receive a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame. Kidjo's career has spanned decades. She's earned a whopping 17 Grammy nominations, winning five of them, and she's collaborated with stars ranging from Alicia Keys to Bono to Quavo.
At her ceremony, there was singing, dancing, there were tears. Here's some of what Kidjo had to say.

The star for me means that my vision of the world as a small village is a reality. We have the same needs, doesn't matter where we come from, which language we speak, which skin color we have. We are human. It's one human family. I don't believe in any other person telling me otherwise.
Kidjo's impact extends far beyond music. She's served as a UNICEF Goodwill Ambassador since 2002 and co-founded the Batonga Foundation, which works to empower girls and young women in Africa.

Now from one superstar to some of you superstars,shout out to Coach Gillette at St. Andrew's Middle School in Columbia, South Carolina. Thank you for sharing some of your students' assignments with us, and congrats on being named Coach of the Year. That is awesome.

This next shout out goes to Mr. Schaefer at Green Hill High School in Mount Juliet, Tennessee. Thank you for making us a part of your day, and be sure to send us some pictures of that pizza party. Happy Friday Eve.
Go make someone smile. It costs you nothing, only takes a moment, and it just may be the spark of joy someone needs. I'll see you tomorrow.
I'm Coy Wire, and we are CNN 10.

title: How primate 'whisperers' are helping safeguard India's biggest events
en: What's up, sunshine? Welcome to the show. I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10.

Happy Friday. If your week was anything like mine, you were feeling the heat, feeling some pressure, and you put in the time to get through. But heat, pressure, and time, the same things that test our fortitude, also make diamonds.
So let's rise up, shine bright, and get your 10 minutes of news.

Now, we begin with potentially groundbreaking news in the fight against cancerinvolving a vaccine. An experimental mRNA vaccine has shown promising results in late-stage clinical trials aimed at preventing the return of melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer.

Results of the ongoing study have shown that when combined with an immunotherapy drug, the vaccine prevented the cancer from returning or spreading among high-risk patients. It uses the same basic mRNA technology that became widely known through COVID-19 vaccines. mRNA, or messenger RNA, carries genetic instructions that tell our cells how to make proteins.

Now, vaccines, particularly mRNA vaccines, are a source of skepticism for some people, and it's important to point out this treatment is still experimental. The complete trial data have not yet been released, and regulators still have to evaluate it.

They take the mRNA that codes for those mutations in the patient's actual tumor, and they give that back to the patient, and the patient makes antibodies to their own tumors. This is a customized, personalized vaccine to treat your own tumor.
So, promising? Absolutely. Proven cure? No.

But potentially an entirely new chapter in how doctors fight cancer. More than 1.5 million Americans were living with melanoma in 2023, according to the National Cancer Institute. Pharmaceutical companies Moderna and Merck, who are co-developing the treatment, say they plan to file for approval from regulators within months.

This weekend, Washington, D.C. becomes Washington of horsepower.The nation's capital is set to transform into a bona fide racetrack, hosting its first ever IndyCar race, the Freedom 250 Grand Prix. The 125-lap race carries a roughly $35 million price tag, all paid for by IndyCar, making it among the most expensive races on their calendar.

Extensive construction was needed to allow open-wheel IndyCars to race safely at speeds of up to 180 miles per hour, including walls to protect both racers and spectators in viewing areas along the track.

The roughly one-and-a-half-mile circuit is centered around the National Mall, and flanked by some of the capital's biggest landmarks. It even features a Pennsylvania Avenue pit lane just blocks from the Capitol Building.

The one-of-a-kind race rounds out a summer of celebrations that included a mixed martial arts fight on the White House lawn, a fair on the National Mall, and what was billed as the biggest fireworks display in history.
Pop quiz, hot shot.Which of these is an actual feature of the rhesus macaque, the monkey commonly found around Delhi, India?
A second stomach, cheek pouches, retractable claws, or a prehensile tail?

Answer is cheek pouches. It's like their own snack pack. Rhesus macaques can stuff food into expandable pouches inside their cheeks and save it for later. The pouches can expand roughly the size of their stomach, basically a lunchbox built into their face.

In the streets of Delhi, India, organizers of the Badminton World Championships have hired people with one of the strangest job descriptions we've ever heard of. Professional monkey whisperer, our Ivan Watson, has more on how they're trying to keep monkeys away from one of badminton's biggest stages.
How do you keep the monkeys that roam New Delhi's streets out of an international sports event? One solution might involve a monkey whisperer.

Here's a monkey whisperer shared by Radio India at Delhi's Indira Gandhi Stadium, where Badminton's World Championships are currently being held. He's imitating the call of a langur monkey to scare away smaller rhesus macaque monkeys.
For years, authorities here have been trying to come up with ways to keep Delhi's monkeys from infiltrating major events without hurting the animals.

They put up life-sized cutouts of langurs when Delhi hosted the G20 summit in 2023. And during the Commonwealth Games in 2010, officials actually employed live langurs to scare away monkeys. But that's illegal now.

A monkey was spotted at Indira Gandhi Stadium at a different badminton event earlier this year. When asked what to do if it happens again this week, the head of India's main badminton association joked, maybe he'll just give the monkey a banana.
Now to Panama, where conservationists just found something that hasn't been documented in this community in nearly three decades.

Tracks in the sand leading to a nest belonging to the biggest sea turtle on the planet. Community conservationists say they've located a leatherback sea turtle nest near Jaqué on Panama's Pacific coast for the first time in nearly 30 years. Officials say at least one leatherback turtle came ashore after conservationists discovered its tracks in the sand.

From 1998 to 2026, we have significantly increased the sea turtle population here. Previously, only one species, the loggerhead, was found here. But now, of the five species found in Panama, four have already arrived in the region.
The turtle's return marks major progress for the town, where conservationists have spent close to two decades dedicating their time to protecting the animals.

Imagine studying for one of the biggest tests of your life,passing, and then being told, yeah, we're going to need you to take that again. That's the reality for tens of thousands of college applicants at the National Autonomous University of Mexico, Mexico's largest university and one of Latin America's most prestigious.

It annulled the results of around 3,000 tests after the results showed an unusually high number of perfect scores, suggesting some students may have cheated using AI. 58,000 applicants were called to take a new test, even if they were not accused of cheating, this time in person and under strict supervision. CNN's Valeria Leon reports.

After an alleged AI fraud using in the admission exam, thousands of students are now lined up to get to this admissions test for the second time to get into the National Autonomous University in Mexico, one of the oldest and most prestigious universities of Latin America.
This is the first time that the UNAM applied this test online and after this fraud allegedly signaling students using AI for this first test, the university decided to reapply this test.
And this is what the students feel of retaking the exam.

Around 50,000 students have presented this test, the second one for the admission to the National Autonomous University, the UNAM. And here in Mexico City, this is the place, Palacio de los Deportes, where thousands of students and also their families, as you can see here, they are waiting for hours until their students can present the test and finally go out. This is the last date for the students to get inside and get this test done and finally get a place in one of the most important universities in Mexico.

Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10, a mama bear who would do anything for her son, including getting some serious ink. 11 year old Hunter Fletcher has nonverbal autism and communicates using augmentative and alternative communication or AAC, a virtual tablet with words and symbols. But when the device's battery died, mom had to try something new.

I got a piece of paper and I wrote the alphabet and he kind of got a little frustrated. He flipped it over and started writing the keyboard and he fake typed on the keyboard to tell me what he wanted to eat.
Inspired by that one afternoon at a restaurant, Fletcher decided to permanently tattoo a keyboard on her arm.
That sparked the idea for me that I can't limit him to technology because technology does fail us.

One viral social media video later, the Fletcher family has now partnered with a clothing company to sell shirts with keyboards on their sleeve. A mom giving a whole new meaning to wearing your heart on your sleeve.
Let's end with some Friday fun. We have a shout out going to Mr. Taylor at Lorain Preparatory High School in O-H-I-O. Thank you for commenting and subscribing on our CNN 10 YouTube channel.
And this shout out goes to Liz Angley at Graded, the American school of Sao Paulo, Brazil. Thank you so much for sending us this very sweet flag and this little dude. Bom dia, brother.
Play that Friday music, Nadir. Go out, have an awesome weekend. Go out, make someone smile.
You never know how or when or who, but you may be the spark of joy someone needs. I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10.
It's been a blessing to spend this week with you.
