title: Special Edition: The Role of the Monarchy, The Role of the Crown
en: What's up, sunshine? Welcome to the show. I'm Coy Wire with a special edition of CNN 10. Today, one royally intriguing topic, all 10 minutes, including a first ever CNN 10 report from one of you, our viewers.

Rise up. Today, we are diving into the difference between the British government and the British crown. The way our friends across the pond run their country, quite different from the way we do things here in the US.
Also, what roles do the king, the queen, and the prince even play? Since it can get confusing, we're going to break it all down.

n the US, the president is both the head of state, the country's symbolic leader, and the head of government, the person who actually runs the executive branch. The president is elected every four years by the people. That means the citizens vote for who they want to be in charge.
In the UK, that's not quite the case. Under a constitutional monarchy, power is divided between the elected government and the ceremonial role of the royal family.
The prime minister is the head of government and runs the country day to day. But here's the twist. Voters don't pick the prime minister directly.
Instead, they vote for a political party, and the party with the most seats in parliament chooses the prime minister. So it's more like voting for the whole team instead of just the captain.
Give this my all, and I ask you all to pull with me. Let's build a new national sense of unity.

Britain also has a monarch, currently King Charles III, who is the head of state. While it is largely a political role, they perform important duties such as officially appointing the prime minister, opening parliament, and providing royal assent to bills signifying that they have become law.

Now that King Charles has taken the throne, his eldest son, William, is the first in line for the crown. And his responsibilities have gotten more and more important for many reasons. Our Max Foster is here to explain.
It used to beall high jinks and banter between William and Harry.
It's pretty rich coming from a ginger, so I'm quite happy to take that moment.
Even after William married, there was plenty of fun to be had in front of the cameras.
But from the moment his grandmother died, he became first in line to the throne, and with that came a more weighty title.
I am proud to create him Prince of Wales to Wysog Cymru.
With that, the new Prince and Princess of Wales have been elevated in position and will now be expected to step up and support the King more.
William's father reinvented the role of Prince of Wales by professionalizing it. The spotlight now firmly on the new Prince and Princess of Wales, the most high profile in history.
While William and his father may attend and officiate many government events, the actual power still lies with the British people.

In America, our politics are mostly divided into a two-party game, Democrats and Republicans. In the United Kingdom, politics plays out a little differently, and with more parties. The two biggest are the Conservatives and the Labour, but there are also several others too, like the Liberal Democrats, the Green Party, and the Scottish National Party.
And as Big Ben strikes 10, the exit poll is predicting a Labour landslide.
In the United Kingdom, elections for Parliament usually happen every five years. Emphasis on usually.

Sometimes, if Parliament can't agree or the government loses a key vote, an early election is called. It's what they call a snap election. Once a majority government has been chosen, Parliament is in charge of making the laws.

The British Parliament is bicameral, meaning it has two chambers. Much like the US has the House of Representatives and the Senate, Britain has the House of Commons and the House of Lords. The Commons members are elected by voters, while the Lords are mostly appointed or have inherited their spots.
The Lords act like experienced advisors. They don't make laws by themselves, but they do review and suggest changes. This system mixes tradition with elected decision-making.

Unlike the US, the UK doesn't have one single written constitution. Instead, its rules come from a mix of important documents, court decisions, and traditions that have developed over centuries, kind of like a recipe passed down through generations. Because it's more flexible, the UK system can adapt over time.
And much like the US, the UK also has a Supreme Court that settles big legal questions and assesses whether new or existing laws follow the country's best interests.

Time for a Did You Know? The London Bridge is not falling down, because it's not even called the London Bridge. And one of you took a vacation to the UK over the summer and filed this special student report.

Hi Coy, I'm in front of Tower Bridge in London, and let me tell you some fun facts about this iconic landmark. Did you know Britain's most famous bridge is actually not called the London Bridge? It's called the Tower Bridge.
The original London Bridge isn't even in London. It was moved brick by brick to Arizona in the 1860s. Two local architects began construction on the bridge April 22, 1886, and it opened in 1894.
Around 31 million bricks were used to construct the bridge, which ended up costing 1 million pounds. That would be about 166 million pounds today. Geez.

Tower bridge is a bascule bridge from the French word from seesaw or balance. Instead of using ropes or chains like a typical drawbridge, the bascules that made up sections of the road moved like two giant seesaws. The sections pivot the bridge open and close, allowing boats to pass through.

Until 1976, the bascules were operated by hydraulics, using steam to power the enormous pumping engines. Today, the bascules are operated by oil and electricity, driven by hydraulic power instead of steam. It takes 206 steps to reach the top of the bridge.
Once there, you could walk between two towers on a glass floor. This addition came in 2014 so that visitors can test their courage and snap some pictures of the river below. Back to you, Coy?

June, that was incredible. Thank you so much for sharing such fascinating facts from your summer vacation. Now, are you traveling somewhere soon or just want to show us around a cool part of your hometown? Send us your own CNN10 field trip video with your parents' permission, of course.
Include your name, age, school, mascot, teacher if you'd like. Send it all to cnn10 at cnn.com. Can't wait to check them out.
Pop quiz, hot shot.
The king of England is not required to have what type of documentation?
Birth certificate, driver's license, checkbook, or passport?

This is actually a twofer. Passports and driving licenses are issued in the name of the monarch, so they don't need to issue one to themselves. Despite his Royal Highness's lack of license, the king is said to have a fleet of luxury vehicles, including vintage Rolls-Royces and Jaguars.

King Charles III took the throne in 2022 after the passing of his mother, Queen Elizabeth II, who ruled for more than 70 years. And while none of you are probably old enough to remember her coronation day, you will likely witness another in your lifetime. Our Randy Kaye explains the significance of the line of succession.

Get in line if you want to be head of the British monarchy. The list of future heirs to the throne includes nearly two dozen members of the royal family. William, the Prince of Wales, is the new heir apparent.

He's the eldest son of King Charles and the late Princess Diana. In 2011, William married Kate Middleton, now the Princess of Wales. They live in a cottage on the grounds of Windsor Castle with their three children, who are next in line behind William.

Their eldest, Prince George of Wales, is second in line to the throne. Princess Charlotte, William and Kate's only daughter, would come after her big brother. Then Prince Louis of Wales, their youngest.

Fifth in line to the throne, Prince Harry, the Duke of Sussex. He's the younger son of King Charles and Diana and William's only sibling. Harry married Meghan Markle in 2018 after they met on a blind date.
They have two children and live in California. Their son, Prince Archie, is in line after his father. His sister, Princess Lilibet, would be next.

Lilibet is seventh in line to the throne. As the Queen's 11th great-grandchild, she is the most senior royal in the line of succession to have been born overseas in California. King Charles' brother, Prince Andrew, is eighth in line despite being stripped of his royal title.

Andrew stepped away from royal duties in 2019. Prince Andrew had married Sarah Ferguson in 1986 and had two daughters before divorcing a decade later. Princess Beatrice, now 34 and ninth in line after her father, gave birth to daughter Sienna Elizabeth Mapelli-Mosey in 2021, who is now tenth in line to the throne.
That makes Princess Eugenie, Beatrice's sister, 11th. Her son, August Philip Hawke, is 12th. Prince Edward, the youngest child of Queen Elizabeth and Prince Philip, is 13th in the line of succession.

Edward's official title is the Earl of Wessex. His two children, James Viscount Severn and his older sister, Lady Louise Mountbatten-Windsor, are in line behind their father. Princess Anne, who was actually the second child born to the Queen and Prince Philip, falls last behind her three brothers and their children.

That's because the 1701 Act of Settlement, which lays down the rules of succession, allowed for younger sons to move ahead of older daughters in line. The 2013 Succession to the Crown Act changed that, but only applies to those born after October 28, 2011. That leaves Princess Anne, 16th in line to the throne.

All right, superstars, that's all for today's special edition. Wherever you are in this world, just know that you are royally awesome, and we are so thankful for you spending part of your day with us. You're our cup of tea.
See you next time. I'm Coy Wire, and we are CNN 10.

title: The African school teaching girls to defy expectations
en: What's up, sunshine? Welcome to the show. I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10.
With your 10 minutes of news, I simply tell you the what, letting you decide what to think. Teacher Time Tuesday this August 25th. Shout out to all the educators inspiring and informing us.
Go and give your teachers some hard hands, a high five or a fist bump today. Let them know I see you. Now, let's get to your news.

We begin in Nevada, where a fast-moving wildfire has sent flames racing towards neighborhoods and tens of thousands of people fleeing their homes.The Hawk Fire exploded to more than 15,000 acres after igniting Saturday. As of this taping, officials say the fire is still 0% contained.

Nevada Governor Joe Lombardo has declared a state of emergency in Washoe County, which includes Reno and parts of Lake Tahoe, and activated the Nevada National Guard. Schools throughout the region were canceled Monday and around 90,000 residents have been urged to evacuate. At least two medical centers have evacuated patients as well.
When we came through, it looked like a movie scene. Like, you don't expect to see something like that in real life.
It's just really scary right now. We've never had to do this before. There was no hotel room at all.

Officials say the fire was human-caused, though exactly how it started remains under investigation. Around 1,000 firefighters are battling the blaze, which has been fueled by gusty winds, low humidity, and dry brush. Those challenging conditions are expected to worsen throughout the week, potentially complicating efforts to contain the fire.
Now to Northwest Indiana,where thousands of families have spent nearly two weeks living without something most of us rarely think about twice, electricity.

Powerful storms knocked down trees, power lines, and hundreds of utility poles August 11th. Initially, more than 300,000 customers lost electricity. As of this taping, more than 20,000 in Gary, Indiana alone were still without power.

That means spoiled food, closed schools, and concerns over refrigerated medicine. Some residents have filed a proposed class action lawsuit against utility company NIPSCO, alleging inadequate tree and vegetation management worsened the outages. NIPSCO says it strongly disagrees, calling the storm damage unprecedented and widespread.
The company says restoration work in hard-hit Gary is expected to be substantially completed by this evening.

Now overseas, where Britain's new prime ministeris making a statement with the destination of his first trip abroad. Prime Minister Andy Burnham traveled to Kiev, Ukraine Monday, meeting President Volodymyr Zelensky and other European leaders.

Burnham also co-chaired a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing, countries working to strengthen Ukraine's security and defense as its war with Russia continues. The timing carried extra significance. Monday was Ukraine's Independence Day, exactly 35 years since the country declared independence from the Soviet Union in 1991.
Pop quiz, hot shot.
Which river in Africa is recognized as the longest in the world? Congo, Nile, Zambezi, or Orange?
If you said Nile, correct. If you said something else, you just might be in denial.
This river boasts 4,132 miles in length and crosses 11 countries, including Egypt, Ethiopia, Sudan, and Kenya.

Imagine being one of just 35 girls chosen from across an entire country, not simply to attend a school, but to challenge generations of expectations. On Senegal's historic Goree Island, an elite boarding school is educating some of the country's brightest young women in a nation where fewer than one in five girls finishes high school.
They're learning that where you begin doesn't have to determine where you end.
At 12, Ndeye Awa Diop says she was too shy to raise her hand in class.
Imagine it. Imagine. I didn't even dare speak in class. I didn't look people in the eye.

At 19, she's now the president of the student council. This is Mariam Abba School of Excellence, an elite girls school on an island off the coast of Senegal. Here, students are encouraged to challenge traditional expectations of women and prepare to become leaders.

But it's an opportunity only a small number of girls get. While the majority of girls in Senegal are enrolled in primary school, less than 20 percent make it through high school, according to United Nations estimates.
We're in a society where there are a lot of prejudices, a lot of obstacles to the emancipation of women.
And in fact, I think that the first rule of life that we teach these girls is that they must get rid of all of these prejudices, assert themselves, and show their leadership wherever they are.
Girls can face pressure to leave school to help at home, marry, or have children. And when families can't afford to educate all their children, boys are often prioritized.

Growing up in rural Senegal, Ndeye Awa Diop experienced this first hand. That is, until she started at this boarding school. The Mariam Abba School has a 100 percent completion rate and tuition is fully funded by the state. They admit 35 girls a year.

Through interacting with people, through listening to advice, through reading as well, through expressing myself, I learned to be a leader, if I can say so. And Diop has. Six years after enrolling, she's about to graduate. She hopes to become an international business lawyer.
For 40 years, UConn women's basketball has been synonymous with one word, winning.

Hall of Fame coach Geno Auriemmahas spent decades bringing together different personalities and perspectives and convincing them to sacrifice for something bigger than themselves. That's at the heart of the new Apple TV docuseries, The Dynasty UConn Huskies. I sat down with coach Auriemmaand Emmy award winning filmmaker Matthew Hamachek.
Coach, when you were approached about this opportunity to tell the story of your career, of your teams, of your program, what was most important to you?

To let everybody see how much people sacrifice to make this work. How much the players themselves gave of themselves to make the team better, gave up individual goals sometimes for the good of the team. How much time was spent on the court? How much time was spent off the court? That this didn't happen by accident. You don't win this much for this long without great people doing amazing things. So I want everybody to see that.

Matthew, your previous series, The Dynasty New England Patriots covered a 20 year run over 10 episodes. Coach Auriemma's UConn dynasty is twice as long. It's still going. How painful was deciding what not to put in this series?
Finding things that make these stories universal.

And if you focus on that, the decisions on what to cut and what not to leave in and things like that become a lot easier. But, you know, it really helps when you have great characters like Coach Auriemma and, you know, Diana Taurasi and Paige Bueckers and all of them to focus on. Because I think when people watch these things, they can see themselves in them.
Even though those characters are going through extraordinary circumstances, the emotions and the things that they're grappling with are very ordinary and universal to all of us.
How did you two work together in the filmmaking process? Who was tougher during this process? Genothe coach or Matthew the filmmaker?

We both knew what we wanted. I wanted my team to win. I wanted my team to look and play like the best team in the country. And I needed to do what I needed to do to make that happen. Matt wanted this to be the best piece that it could be, the best series that it could be.
And he knew what he wanted to make that happen. 90% of the time, those two things were in perfect harmony. The other 10%, you know, that's just normal, par for the course stuff.
But he is annoying. And once you take that for granted, you know, say, look, he's going to be annoying. He's going to be annoying. So just deal with it.
Coach, we saw some of the familiar faces teased in the trailer. Sue Bird, Paige Bueckers, Azzi Fudd, Rebecca Lobo, Maya Moore, Breanna Stewart, Sarah Strong, on and on.
You spent decades telling these women what you thought of them. Now you had to sit here and hear what they thought of you. How uncomfortable, how heartwarming, how enlightening was that for you?

You know, that's a good way to put it. I think it was all those things. It was heartwarming in the sense that the kind of effect that we as coaches have had on those players that have come through here. You know, if you played and you know that that sacred place, that locker room and that team bond, that's real.
And that has an effect on us as coaches, them as players, and that doesn't go away. So it was great to hear that.
Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10 passion, precision, and enough fancy footwork to make your feet file for overtime.

Tango teaches us something. Sometimes you step forward, sometimes you have to step back. The important thing is to keep on moving.

Go find it. I'm Coy Wire, and we are CNN10.

en: What's up, everyone? I'm Coy Wire, this is CNN 10, and it is Your Word Wednesday. Today, you helped us write this show. So listen up for your words as we travel from a history-making vote to history-making football to robots that are now running faster than humans.

Let's get to your news for August 26th. And on this day in history, 1920, American women officially gained the constitutional right to vote. The 19th Amendment was formally certified 106 years ago today.

The amendment prohibits the federal government or any state from denying a citizen the right to vote based on sex. It capped more than 70 years of activism by the women's suffrage movement, led by figures like Susan B. Anthony and Elizabeth Cady Stanton. An estimated 26 million women became eligible to vote in that 1920 U.S. election.
But the amendment didn't make voting equal overnight. Poll taxes, discriminatory local laws, and other barriers continued preventing many women of color from exercising that right for decades.
Now to Iran, where ceasefire negotiations have gone awry.

And amid the fallout from war, women are once again facing increased scrutiny over something deeply personal — what they wear. Social media video delineates women being shamed on the streets, even more so if they don't have the mandated hijab, a headscarf associated with the religious tradition of covering the hair, ears, and neck. Our Jomana Karacha has more on why the crackdown is intensifying now.

This woman is being publicly shamed by another woman for showing her bare legs in Iran. Eventually, officers arrive and make her put on pants. This scene is being played out in cities across the country.

The focus seems to be turning back to how women are allowed to dress. At the height of the war, women without headscarves were even seen at pro-government gatherings. The regime seemed to have bigger priorities, but now hardliners are pushing the hijab back on the agenda.

Cafes, restaurants, and shops are being shut down for failing to enforce mandatory dress codes. Hardline clerics are demanding tougher enforcement. This cleric speaking directly to President Masoud Pezeshkian.

But there's a problem for the regime. Iranian women are not backing down. Four years ago, the death of Mahsa Jina Amini in custody after being detained by the so-called morality police ignited the Women, Life, Freedom protest.

The uprising was brutally suppressed, but widespread acts of defiance survived. Today, women walk through Iranian cities without headscarves and ride motorcycles through Tehran, Shiraz, and Isfahan as the war with the U.S. seems to stall and all confrontation is bubbling up.
Tick, tick, tick, 10-second trivia.
Which of these traits is unique to the big cats that make up the genus Panthera?
Retractable claws, roaring, night vision, or patterned coats?

If you said roaring, you were born to be heard. Like lions, tigers, leopards, and jaguars, the only cats that can roar. And get this, the same bone that allows them to roar also prevents them from purring. And I'm not lying.

To Argentina now, where dozens of lions and tigers have just been rescued from an abandoned zoo, which had become a dangerous tourist attraction. The animals were removed from their overcrowded enclosures and are now being transferred to animal sanctuaries around the globe. Our Isabel Rosales has more.
A chance at a new life. That's what these big cats now have after being moved to new sanctuaries across the world.

At first, we try also not to make radical change, but the quality of life will change. They will have hundreds of square meters. They will have a proper food, a proper medical care. They were forgotten for many years, and I think now it will be a new life for them.
The lions and tigers were rescued from a former zoo near Buenos Aires, shut down by Argentine officials in 2020 over safety concerns. The zoo was known for letting visitors handle the animals.

In 2025, Global Animal Welfare Organization, 4PAWS, took on responsibility for the animals. Veterinarians brought in to treat the big cats said they found many injuries like deformed paws from declawing, kidney disease and open wounds.
We found various injuries on the skin, on the tail, on the ears.So we have some broken canines, which is very common in big cats when they do this bar biting.
Now, 4PAWS sent 30 of them to sanctuaries in the U.S. and South Africa to start their new lives.

When we started with the complete medical examination of all these animals here in Lujan Zoo, based on this examination, we evaluated that there are several animals that need urgent attention and they need to be moved to sanctuaries and places where this is possible to be insured.

This week, 15 of these tigers and lions were taken to Lions Rock Big Cat Sanctuary in South Africa, which is owned by 4PAWS, while the other 15 were transferred to the Wild Animal Sanctuary in Colorado.
I feel well when I reach to my destination with the animal and when I see them, I feel how it is valuable to save a life.

Whether they're in Colorado or South Africa, 4PAWS says these big cats will get to experience life as close to their natural habitat as possible, tailored to their specific needs, and that family groups and lifelong companions will remain together in their new sanctuary homes.
But most importantly, they'll finally be able to get the care they need.
Now to an NFL moment that's bigger than football. History has been made.

Shiyazh Pete has become the first member of the Navajo Nation to play in the NFL. The 6'9 Dallas Cowboys rookie offensive lineman took the field against the Arizona Cardinals in Glendale. Shiyazh was shocked to see thousands of Navajo Nation members in the stands.

When he entered the game in the fourth quarter, helping Dallas score a touchdown, the crowd erupted. His teammates stood to the side to let him have his moment. When asked what he saw, he said, hope and courage. Afterwards, he was celebrated in the locker room by his teammates and his coach.
But I saw something I've never seen before. 25 years in the NFL, an entire section cheering for one man.
This game, fate brought us here as strangers, but this game, this star, this team will make us brothers.

Chinese robots are now beating the apex of humanathletic achievements at this year's World Humanoid Robot Games. It's the second year China has hosted the competition as it aggressively invests in the robotics industry.
But there is far more at stake here than seeing which droid will cross the finish line. Our Mike Valerio reports.
Some astonishing and not so astonishing feats in one of the Olympic stadiums here in Beijing.

The humanoid robot named Lightning ran the hundred meter race faster than Usain Bolt's world record. But you know, these competitors, they don't need protein drinks. They need batteries here at the World Humanoid Robot Games. Robo athletes are being tested like never before.
More than 2000 robots from 16 countries are registered for this year's games. And we have kickboxing, football, table tennis, and some of these events are getting much harder.
The 400 meter race, for example, is now totally autonomous. It's reading these robots need to see the track, navigate it, and cross the finish line without anybody guiding them by remote control.

And this is actually part of the point. When a robot falls, gets confused, or manages to recover on its own, engineers get a real world test of technology they ultimately want working outside the arena.

China's made embodied AI, which is essentially AI in a physical body, a national priority. And the government has backed research training centers and real world testing as so many Chinese universities and companies have raced to build better robot bodies and even smarter robot brains.

So the real competition here isn't just robot versus robot, it's how quickly China can move these machines from spectacle to something a little bit more useful. And judging by what we're seeing here, there are both some amazing achievements and a little bit more training to do.
Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10, a real life example of teamwork that makes the dream work.

In Japan, about 1000 people chosen by lottery were recruited to help move this 400 ton castle back to its original place. Their method, grit, muscle, and a bit of tug of war, the Hirosaki Castle was originally moved in 2015 so workers could repair the stone wall beneath it, which supported the structure. This month's big move traveled a grand total of one meter, around three feet.

But those biceps and triceps will be getting quite a few more reps while the repairs are done. It's expected to take the rest of the year to move this whimsical heavyweight back to its original footprint. That's a monumental move, literally.

All right, we have an extra special Your Word Wednesday today because our friends at the Stratton School in Maine sent us this vocabulary adventure book. First up, delineate. Did you hear that word in the show? A verb that means to precisely describe, portray, or outline something in detail. I see you, Jasper. Kind of like that purple jacket.
We also worked in awry, an adjective or adverb that means not going according to plan. Emma, great word. Absolutely love it.
Finally, Autumn gave us one of my favorite words, whimsical, which means playful, imaginative, or fanciful in an unusual way.
You all made us smarter today by delineating each of these words. May your imaginations be full of whimsy and your plans never go awry. Stay curious, my friends.
I'm Coy Wire, and we are CNN 10.

title: Remembering the life and legacy of Dolly Parton
en: What's up, sunshine? I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10. Today we have a Louisiana launch pad reaching for the stars, AI trying to top the charts, and a baby shark who's all grown up.
Ten minutes, big world. Let's dive in. We start with two quotes, full of wisdom.

Find out who you are and do it on purpose. And if you see someone without a smile, give them yours. Words to live by from iconic singer, songwriter, and philanthropist Dolly Parton, who died this week at the age of 80.
Known around the world as the queen of country music, or simply Dolly, the one-of-a-kind star rose from humble beginnings in rural Tennessee to become one of the biggest names in music history.

But for all the records she sold and awards she won, Dolly's greatest hit may have been the lives she touched. She leaves a remarkable legacy of philanthropy, proof that sometimes the biggest stars shine brightest on other people. Our Mina Doerson has more, and a look back at Dolly's incredible career and enduring impact.
Well, I wanted to be a star, but I always thought of a star more of as a singing star.
Legendary country music star, businesswoman, actor, and philanthropist Dolly Parton has died. Parton was born one of 12 kids in a one-bedroom cabin in East Tennessee.
I was never ashamed of my background, even though we grew up very poor.
Those humble beginnings would shape her life in music.
I think we've become who we are when we're young.
By 21, Parton broke into the country billboard charts for the first time with her single, Dumb Blonde.

It was one of the first milestones in a career that spanned seven decades. She released over 50 albums, winning 10 Grammys, and garnering 55 Grammy nominations, the most ever for a female country artist.
She received an honorary Oscar in 2025 for her humanitarian work.
It makes me want to dream up new ways to help lift people up, and isn't that what we're supposed to be here for?
Opening Dollywood, a theme park near her hometown in East Tennessee that employs thousands and has invigorated the surrounding area.
Hundreds and hundreds of businesses have sprung up and thousands and thousands of jobs. I just really think business. I get that from my dad.
Parton supported many charitable causes, including childhood literacy through her imagination library.
We've officially gifted over 200 million books to children.
Dolly Parton leaves behind more than iconic music. She leaves a legacy of generosity, humility, and a reminder to be kind to one another.
I think everybody should be treated with respect. I hope that everybody gets a chance to be who and what they are.
Elon Musk's SpaceX says it's planning to build what could become the biggest rocket launch site on Earth in Louisiana.

SpaceX unveiled plans for a massive $100 billion spaceport near Louisiana's Gulf Coast. Construction is expected to begin next year, with the first launch targeted for 2029. They are calling it Starbase Louisiana, a play off SpaceX's existing starbase in South Texas, where the company develops and tests its massive Starship rocket.

And get this, Musk says the Louisiana site could eventually have more than a dozen launch towers capable of supporting more than 30 flights each day. That's more like an airport departure schedule. But before anyone starts packing for Mars, this thing still has to get off the ground here on Earth.
The enormous project faces regulatory and environmental reviews particularly significant because it would be built along Louisiana's ecologically sensitive Gulf Coast.
Pop quiz hot shot. Which country has produced the most number one hits on America's Billboard Hot 100 by artists born outside the U.S.? Australia, Canada, United Kingdom, or Sweden?
If you said the United Kingdom, ding ding! Correct.

The Brits have been topping the charts for decades. Down under, there is a new debate about who or what deserves a spot on the charts. In Australia, artificial intelligence is shaking up the music charts and stirring up some very human controversy.

The Australian Recording Industry Association, known as ARIA, announced this week that music generated entirely by AI will no longer be eligible for its official charts, ranking the country's biggest songs. The decision follows controversy surrounding an Australian DJ's AI-assisted cover of Madonna's Like a Prayer, which became a chart hit. Apparently AI was living on a prayer, ARIA said, not on our chart.

The organization says the goal is to protect the human nature of artistry. Important distinction, AI isn't completely banned. Recordings that use generative AI in a supporting role will still be eligible.
We're just not really interested in celebrating the success of AI-generated music, and particularly when it takes the spot of an Australian artist in our charts.

The move comes amid a broader fight over music rights in the age of AI, with organizations like the Recording Industry Association of America and the Grammys pushing for stricter scrutiny over AI-produced tracks.

So what do you think? Should entirely AI-generated music be allowed to compete against songs created and performed by humans? How would you balance technological advancements while staying true to an artist's vision? Feel free to press pause and ruminate solo or discuss with friends. Preferably human ones.

Now to a promising new development in the world of medicine. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration, or FDA, has cleared a new blood test to help identify signs of Alzheimer's disease in people aged 55 and older with cognitive decline.

It allows doctors to use biomarkers to help identify patients who are likely or unlikely to have Alzheimer's-related brain changes. Alzheimer's is a fatal progressive brain disorder where protein fragments called amyloid plaques build up in the brain, causing cell death and brain damage. The disease affects more than 7 million Americans and is one of the leading causes of death in those over 65.

The test, which was developed by pharmaceutical companies Roche and Eli Lilly, received approval in Europe earlier this year. While no price has been announced, Roche says it can be run on more than 4,500 existing labs across the country.
Biomarker blood tests offer a possible alternative to traditionally expensive and invasive procedures used to identify the disease, including brain scans and spinal taps.

If you think this summer's been hot, imagine wearing a fur coat all day.In Tokyo, where extreme summer temperatures have been downright rough, a fan-powered suit is helping dogs beat the heat. Our Scout Richards has more on one seriously fetching invention.

These are some hot dogs, and this invention is supposed to cool them down. Yes, those are tiny battery-powered fans strapped to a dog. The puffy pet jackets were created by Tokyo-based maternity wear company Sweet Mommy as Japan swelters through extreme summer heat.
I have never lived in a hotter country than here. It is very dangerous even for us humans and for dogs who cannot sweat like us. It's even worse.

So how does this thing actually work? Two battery-powered fans pull air into the jacket, while an ice pack in the collar helps cool the air before it circulates around the animal's body. And apparently there's a market for canine cooling. Sweet Mommy says it has sold nearly 10,000 of the pet suits since launching the first version in 2022. The latest model costs about $104.
Yeah, I'm very excited that there is at least one brand here that thinks about the well-being of our fur babies in such conditions.
Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10, Baby Shark gets a glow up.

The seven-year-old boy featured in the most viewed video in YouTube history is now a K-pop star, has been playing in the White House, launched countless trends, and racked up more than 17 billion views on YouTube. It's Baby Shark Dance, and one of the video's stars is now starting a music career of his own. Park Geon-roung, known as Baby Shark Boy, released his debut single, Wave, which begins with a melody that might sound a little familiar.
Baby Shark Boy says the song represents a new beginning for him as an artist. Here is hoping his career has some serious bite. All right, that's about all we have for our show today.
But before we go, you know what time it is. It is shout-out time. This one goes to Mr. Marshall at Shippensburg High School in my home state of Pennsylvania.
Thank you for subscribing and commenting on our CNN10 YouTube channel and leaving such a kind comment. I miss all my wrestling and football days up there at Shippensburg.
And this next shout-out goes to Ms. Pomikpik at Yamato Colony School in Livingston, California.

They made this custom puzzle of their class watching the show, and I was a bit puzzled at first as to why there was a piece missing. And I'm thinking, first of all, that is very sweet. Second of all, if that's supposed to be me, you found me.
Shine on, sunshine. That's our 10 for the day. Be curious, be kind, and remember, you don't have to change the world today.
Just make your corner shine a little brighter. I'm Coy Wire, and we are CNN10.

title: Do you have Instagram? The "transformational" changes coming for teens
en: Happy Friday, Fri-yay! I'm Coy Wire with your CNN 10 minutes of news. And before we get to the weekend, let's finish this week strong. Big stories, big questions, and thousands of people throwing tomatoes at each other. Yeah, we've got you covered.

Today on The 10, we start with a major legal development that could change the landscape of social media. Facebook and Instagram parent company, Meta, has agreed to pay roughly $18 billion to resolve a multi-state lawsuit claiming the company intentionally designed addictive platforms that harmed young people's mental health.

The settlement involves dozens of states and territories and requires Meta to make changes aimed at protecting users under the age of 18. Our Claire Duffy explains what could change and what it can mean for millions of us who scroll, swipe, and share. Hello, Claire.

Hey, Coy. Yeah, this really could be a turning point in how young people are protected on social media. These are the kinds of changes that parents and advocates, and even some teens themselves, have been calling on the social media platforms to make.

Now, Meta agreed to this settlement midway through a trial where just four of those state attorneys general had been seeking as much as $1 trillion in damages. That would have been a huge number. This $18 billion settlement is still a really significant number.

Some of these state attorneys have pointed out that this is the largest settlement with a big tech company in history. That money will go towards helping the states fund youth mental health programs, online safety trainings. But even more important here, I think, is the changes that Meta has agreed to make to its platforms.
I'll walk you through some of those. Teens ages 13 to 17 will now have a two-hour daily time limit across Facebook and Instagram. Only parents will be able to change that.

These platforms are also implementing a night mode, so teens will be unable to access them from midnight to 6 a.m., a school mode, so teens will be getting fewer notifications throughout the day. Meta is turning off likes on teens' content and removing access to extreme beauty filters. And it will also send teens prompts every 15 minutes to make them think a little bit more about how much they're using these platforms.

And very importantly, Coy, both Meta and the state attorneys general here are calling on TikTok and YouTube to make similar changes. Meta has said, we'll pay 70% of this $18 billion sort of upfront, but the other 30% is contingent on TikTok and YouTube making similar changes. The state attorneys general have said they are willing to go after those platforms in court if they don't come to the table voluntarily to make these changes to their platforms.
So this really could be a watershed moment in terms of changing how young people are able to interact on social media. Coy?
This next report comes with a warning. We're going to show images of a deadly natural disaster that some of you may find difficult to watch.

If you'd rather not see them, you can fast forward about two minutes. Catastrophic flash floods, devastated communities along the Nepal-China border, rescue crews are searching for people still missing, the flooding destroyed roads, knocked out power, and entire communities were cut off from help. Our Hanako Montgomery has more on how these floods weren't even caused by rain, but rather a massive Himalayan glacier that collapsed.

Dozens of people begin to run. What comes next in this surveillance video is hard to imagine. A mountain of mud and water, taller than the building, crashes down, wiping out everything in its path, like something from a disaster film.

But this is a border crossing between China and Nepal. It's the result of a deadly flash flood that swept through Himalayan villages on the Nepal-China border on Wednesday. It's enormous force destroying homes and buildings, including in Nepal's Rasuwa district.

Aerial footage captured from a helicopter over the district shows the immense barrage of water flooding the valley below. It's a popular area for hiking holidays. Hundreds of tourists, including foreign nationals, have been reported missing, according to an initial assessment by Nepal's tourism board.

Nepalese army helicopters are helping rescue citizens from rooftops in the flood-affected areas. The Red Cross is also deploying an emergency team with relief supplies. And in Tibet's Gyirong port, China's President Xi Jinping has ordered all-out search and rescue efforts to find those who are missing after a mudslide caused major casualties, China's state news agency Xinhua reported.

The mudslide has cut off the region's roads, communications, and power, Xinhua said. Nepal's foreign minister said the deadly flash flood was caused by an earthquake, triggering a large landslide which blocked the Bhotekoshi river. The full scale of the devastation is yet to become clear.
Pop quiz, hot shot. What special ability do dolphins use to find objects even when they can't see them?
Telepathy, telekinesis, fin language, or echolocation?
If you said echolocation, yeah that was rough. Dolphins send out rapid clicks and for the echoes that bounce back.
It's basically biological sonar. Our news assistant Ankit says he uses it to find free snacks.
According to Greek legend, Taras, the son of the sea god Poseidon, survived a shipwreck after being rescued by a dolphin.

Now, thousands of years later, an Italian city named for the fabled figure is returning the favor. Taranto, situated in Italy's heel-of-the-boot region of Puglia, will host Europe's first sea-based sanctuary for formerly captive dolphins. The sprawling sanctuary along the Ionian Sea will cover about 7 hectares, or 13 NFL football fields.

Formerly captive dolphins at aquariums will be able to live in a protected section of the actual sea. Think of it as going from a swimming pool to an oceanfront neighborhood. Many dolphins raised in captivity can't simply be released into the wild because they may lack the survival skills needed to find food or avoid danger.

So, researchers hope sanctuaries like this can offer something in between human care with floating offices, veterinary platforms, and AI-powered underwater monitoring systems helping scientists study the animals around the clock.
The arts community is mourning the passing of two icons inrecent weeks. Neither seemed particularly interested in being ordinary.

Famed British actor Tim Curry and groundbreaking Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama. Curry became one of the biggest names in Hollywood for his flamboyant characters and unmatched charisma. He died Tuesday at the age of 80.

He exploded onto screens with cult classics like The Rocky Horror Picture Show and Clue. He played cranky hotel concierge in Home Alone 2, sailed alongside Muppets as Long John Silver, and terrified folks as Pennywise the Clown. What. A. Range.
Curry suffered a major stroke in 2012 but continued working, particularly as a voice actor.
And groundbreaking Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama spent nearly a century seeing the world differently and invited the rest of us inside.

Born in Japan in 1929, she endured a difficult childhood, working in a military factory sewing parachutes for Japan's Imperial Army during World War II. She began experiencing vivid hallucinations as a child, involving dots, patterns, and flashes. But instead of hiding them, she transformed them into art.

Polka dots became her trademark, and as my family and I found out, it is magical. Her famous infinity mirror rooms, they allow you to step inside the art. Feels like somebody picked you up and dropped you into another universe.
Kusama passed away August 14th at the age of 97.
All right, today's story, getting a 10 out of 10. It's messy, it's saucy, and it's the only day a year when you can throw your lunch at thousands of strangers and it's apparently encouraged.
Welcome to La Tomatina. Thousands descended on the tiny Spanish town of Buñuel, all for the world's biggest food fight on Wednesday. Overripe tomatoes went airborne.

Splat, squish, sauce everywhere, painting the town red, and here's your knowledge bomb. Afterwards, the streets were hosed down, and because of the tomato's citric acid acting as a cleaning agent, the town streets were actually left cleaner than before. That's one way to catch up on your cleaning.

It is finally Friday, and before I go, I want to give a shout out, and this one goes to Mrs. Guerrero Medrano at Fly Junior High School in Crystal City, Texas. You so fly, and so am I, because of the coolest poncho I ever did see, and it's good for fishing tomatoes off YouTube.
This next shout out goes to Miss Barnett at Oak Grove Middle School in Winston-Salem, North Carolina.

Your former student-turned-fellow teacher, Mr. Oakley, nominated you and wanted to say thank you for your more than 30 years of teaching. Think about all of the lives you have inspired. Congrats on your upcoming retirement.
Play that Friday music, Nadir. This is going to be the best weekend, because it's the next weekend. Make your moments count.
Make someone smile, because you never know when or how, but you may be the spark of joy someone needs. I'm Coy Wire, this is CNN 10. It's been a blessing to spend this week with you.

title: NASA's newest 'discovery machine' could change our understanding of the universe
en: What's up, sunshine? I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10. Today we are traveling from the birth of movies to a telescope, looking back toward the birth of the universe.
History, mystery, and a whole lot of curiosity. Let's get smarter. Lights, camera, action.

129 years ago today, one of history's most famous inventors helped shape the future of motion pictures. On August 31st, 1897, Thomas Edison received a patent for his motion picture camera, the Kinetograph, predecessor to modern projectors. It was cutting-edge technology for its time, capturing a rapid sequence of images onto strips of celluloid film.

And when those pictures were viewed rapidly, one after another, bam, your brain perceived motion. While Edison is credited with the patent, here is your history knowledge bomb. Edison didn't do it alone.

His assistant, William Kennedy Laurie Dickson, is credited with the bulk of the experimentation and development, a reminder that some of history's greatest individual inventions were actually team sports. The Kinetograph helped pave the way for the development of movie projectors, theaters, and the entertainment experience we know and love today. Somewhere Edison's probably like, I should have patented popcorn, too.

A new eye in the sky has just launched into the cosmos.To help us better understand the mysteries of space, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope blasted off Sunday from Kennedy Space Center aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket. Over the next five years, the bus-sized telescope will seek out otherwise invisible and faint space objects.
And liftoff. Go Falcon Heavy and go Roman Space Telescope. And liftoff.

Is basically cosmic panorama mode. Roman is able to survey the sky up to 1,000 times faster than the famous Hubble telescope across a field of view about a hundred times larger, and it's expected to help answer some of science's biggest questions about dark matter and dark energy.
U.S. President Donald Trump has signed an executive order beginning the process of creating a new U.S. Space Academy.

Think Naval Academy with a lot more rocket science. The proposed Academy would recruit and train aspiring astronauts, physicists, engineers, and aerospace technicians, among others. The president announced the move in Houston, Texas, while presenting the Artemis 2 crew with the Congressional Space Medal of Honor.

He said the U.S. Space Academy would train personnel for the Space Force and NASA, while also supporting the civilian space industry like SpaceX and Blue Origin. Important distinction, the executive order creates a commission to figure out how to make the Academy happen.
To Nepal now, where as of this taping,more than 3,000 people are reported missing after that catastrophic flooding and landslide along the Chinese-Nepali border.

The death toll has risen to at least 750 people. Rescue crews are running into changing landscapes, as another landslide on Saturday created a new barrier lake near the disaster zone. The rescuers, themselves, had to be evacuated from the area.

Almost a thousand workers are also missing across a slew of hydropower projects in Nepal. In one of the tunnels, rescuers are pumping air in and dropping food, but haven't connected with anyone inside yet. Among the missing are foreign nationals from around the world.
CNN's Will Ripley found one American couple who narrowly escaped the flood while on a tour bus.
It was violent. It was aggressive. Aggressive with anger. That's how I saw the water come. So I really asked him, I mean, why is God so angry with us?
Anjana Raja and Putupi Venkatesan came to Nepal from Northern California for a spiritual journey, but not one like this.
Just seeing so many people die, I think that's going to last for a while. It's going to linger for a while. I don't know if we will get over it anytime soon.
They were on a tour bus near the China-Nepal border, about to cross into Tibet, when people outside started running and screaming. There was no time to think. Our reflexes needed to be so fast.

I saw something coming really brown up there going up like 60 to 70 feet, something coming brown our way. At that point, I didn't know whether it was water or whether it was dust. So the way it came is came just like a tsunami, just came going all the way up.
And just like a tsunami, how it sweeps going like a row, it just took the buses, the houses, people, everything.
They shared this photo showing what's left of their tour bus.

It's very hard to express in words. A lot of turmoil inside. It was nerve-wracking, especially when you see death just five seconds away from you. I thought about everybody who lost their lives there.
He's a lifesaver, my brother. Their tour guide, Dashi Tumang, guided them up the mountain with just seconds to spare.
How can running, you know? Just running, just running. 10 seconds, it's finished. 10 seconds, everything's underwater. Oh my God, oh my God.
After running to higher ground, they spent the night huddling in the woods with a small group of survivors.

There are about 70, 80 people in that little area. We got to put our bags, sit on the bag. That's about it. You know, we had like two inch wiggle room. We couldn't move more than two inches because it was so full. Water all night, little or no food. We had to share water, whoever had water.
Finally, a helicopter came to rescue them.
And here you are now, and you have your temporary passport. You're going to go home and see your daughter and your son. I can't wait.
Can't wait. What do you want to say to them? What are you going to do when you see them? I'm going to hug them and cry because I am an emotional mama. I am going to hug them and cry.

And I'm just thankful to God that I'm alive and there for them. I'm going to tell them, take life seriously and be ready for whatever comes. This is a learning. Things could happen to anyone. It could happen to us again. So be ready. I'm going to tell them that.
10 Second Trivia.What year was Little League Baseball founded?
1924, 1939, 1953, or 1961? Tick, tick, tick, tick.

If you said 1939, play ball. Little League was founded by Carl E. Stotz in Williamsport, Pennsylvania. It's become a global sensation, played by approximately 2 million 10 to 12-year-olds across 80 different countries.

This year's Little League Baseball World Series is officially in the books. Congrats to Curacao capturing its second Little League World Series championship after defeating Nevada. The Caribbean powerhouse punched its ticket after shutting out Japan for nothing in the international championship.

Curacao is the only Caribbean nation ever to win the Little League Baseball World Series. Nevada reached the final after beating Ohio 12 to 2 in Saturday's U.S. championship game. That's where 12-year-old Carsynn Meyer became the first girl ever to play in the U.S. championship game.

And she drove in a run. How's that for seizing your moment? The Little League World Series is an annual reminder that we're never too young to chase greatness. From legendary names like Gary Sheffield, Jason Varitek, and Todd Frazier to present-day All-Stars, some of baseball's biggest names appeared in the tournament long before reaching the biggest stage.

In 2007, future three-time All-Star and 2019 NL MVP Cody Bellinger helped lead his Chandler, Arizona team to the semifinals at just 11 years old. 13 years later, he hoisted the World Series trophy as a Los Angeles Dodger. More than 70 tournament alumni have reached the majors. Pretty cool reminder.
We never know where the field we're playing on right now might eventually lead, so keep dreaming big. Today's story getting a 10 out of 10.

Two mechanics proving that sometimes the most important thing you can fix is not the car, it's somebody's day. At the Junkie Garage in Glendale, Arizona, 17-year-old Matthew Cuba and his dad, Mike, fix cars for veterans, single parents, seniors, and others in need of free or low-cost repairs. The idea started after financial struggles forced Mike to learn how to repair his own car.

Customers can bring their own parts, and the father-son team provides the labor. Sometimes Matthew and Mike buy parts themselves when a customer simply can't afford them. Their Facebook supporters can chip in a couple dollars a month helping the Cubas help others.
For us, it's about helping people who can never repay that favor.
It makes me feel like a superhero in a way. I mean, I'm helping people that otherwise wouldn't have had any solution.
They're fixing brakes, engines, and maybe even restoring a little faith in humanity.
All right, superstars, two shout-outs for you today on this last day of August. This first one goes to Mrs. J. Rodriguez at Grizzly Challenge Charter School in San Luis Obispo, California.
Tough times can make us tougher. We can learn strength from our struggles. Rise up, and thank you for making us a part of your day.
And this shout-out goes to Mr. Bennett at Most Holy Redeemer School in Evergreen Park, Illinois. And speaking of rise up, thank you for my new favorite shirt. Check it out.
Shine on, sunshine. Stay curious, stay kind, and wherever you go today, bring some light with you. I'm Coy Wire, and we are CNN 10.

title: Seeing red: This unique festival celebrates the world's rarest hair color
en: Badia! Dancing in September! What's up, sunshine? I'm Coy Wire, and a brand new month means 30 new chances to learn something, try something, and treat someone with kindness. 10 minutes, big world, let's start this month strong.
September 1st marks the beginning of meteorological fall in the northern hemisphere and meteorological spring in the southern hemisphere.

So depending on where you're watching us, either grab the pumpkin spice or start smelling the flowers, and let's get to the news. All right, we begin at one of Earth's greatest natural wonders, where nature has given us another reminder of just how quickly beauty can become dangerous. A devastating flash flood tore through parts of the Grand Canyon National Park Saturday.
Dozens of hikers and campers were evacuated, many by helicopter. Approximately 15 people were still missing as of this taping. At least one person had died.

One hiker described a wall of debris rushing toward their group, waterfalls suddenly appearing, boulders tumbling, and landslides erupting around them. The flooding struck the Bright Angel Creek corridor after intense thunderstorms. Popular hiking and camping areas have been closed.

The Grand Canyon plunges more than a mile deep in places and exposes rocks approaching 2 billion years old. More than 4.4 million people visited last year. And the disaster is another reminder that flash floods can happen quickly, especially in narrow canyons where water has nowhere else to go.

Now to an update on the conflict in the Middle East. U.S. Central Command says American forces struck two Iranian rocket launchers in Larak Island Sunday. The U.S. military says Iranian Revolutionary Guard forces were preparing to use rockets to deploy sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz.

Just days before, U.S. President Donald Trump warned Iran against placing new mines in the Strait, and the U.S. military said it had just finished clearing mines from international shipping lanes there. Roughly one-fifth of the world's oil supply has historically traveled through this narrow passage. Iran responded by firing ballistic missiles toward two U.S. bases in Jordan.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard called the Americans strike a, quote, strategic and deadly mistake, unquote. This was the first publicly confirmed direct exchange of fire between U.S. and Iranian forces in about a month.
Pop quiz hot shot about what percentage of the world's population has naturally red hair?
2%, 8%, 15, or 25? If you said 2%, you're red hot.
Natural red hair is one of the world's rarest hair colors. It's most common among people with Northern and Northwestern European ancestry.
Once a year, thousands of redheads from more than 80 countries come together in the city of Tilburg, Netherlands, to celebrate their uniqueness at the Dutch Redhead Days Festival.

And get this, in 2005, Dutch artist Bart Rouwenhorst put on an advertisement looking for a handful of red-haired models. Instead, hundreds responded. So rather than tell most of them no, he invited them all, and an international festival was born. Our Ben Hunt has more.

Seeing red? That is the beauty of the Redhead Days Festival in the Netherlands. It's estimated that less than 2% of the world's population has naturally red hair, and attendees say it's a rare chance to be surrounded by people with similar roots.

Every year, the Dutch city of Tilburg turns into a sea of ginger, copper, and strawberry. The three-day event draws thousands of redheads from all around the world for a chance to show off their locks.
It's just a really cool thing, seeing so many people, it's just really cool.
And enjoy music, food, and specialized workshops that cover everything from skin cancer prevention to makeup tips.
I was inspired to create a product for redheads because we can't find redhead mascaras and for brows, so we made a little makeup booth.
Though red is the star of this show, organizers say everyone is invited. Because the camaraderie and positive energy of the event is enough to make anyone blend in.
You don't have to be a redhead to be welcome, because we just celebrate the humanness and like the unique points of a human being. We just celebrate it.

From people standing out in a crowd to students preparing to stand out in the sky. Birds flying high, you know how they feel, because one New York City high school is helping students explore careers in the aviation industry, learning everything from airplane mechanics to air traffic control, and after graduating, they are fully equipped to take flight.
There's a lot of opportunity in this aviation that a lot of high schools don't have.
All right, you can tell me how this purchase works.

Aviation High School is a public New York City high school that is also a federal aviation administration regulated aviation maintenance school. We are one of the largest in the country, all the traditional high school coursework, plus hands-on work that can get them a job in the aviation industry right after high school.

At aviation, students learn every aspect of the plane. They specialize in certifications that allow them to succeed in careers in aircraft management and manufacturing, taking on roles as airplane mechanics, air traffic controllers, and flight dispatchers as soon as they graduate.

We want to make sure that they're in class every day, that they're studying every day, that they're getting all their jobs done properly, because again, there's people's lives at stake when they get into the workforce to work on the airplanes that we all fly on.

You know, there's like so many different parts of the plane that you really need to have some idea of each section, and really every single class prepares you somewhat for that for that road into the aviation field.
Like other career and technical high schools, Aviation High struggles with recruiting women. In fact, women make up less than 10% of all skilled trade jobs across the country.

I think in any class I'm in, there's less than 10 girls in that class. Every day, I feel like I have to prove myself, and that's hard, but it's very rewarding when I finish at the same pace that the boys do.

Getting into Aviation High isn't easy. In 2023, just over 4,000 applicants competed for only 500 seats at the school. Students travel by train, bus, and ferry from all over New York City, commuting up to two and a half hours to attend the school.

So it's very early mornings. Sometimes, like currently, I have to be here about like 6.30, because I'm coming to practice in for my licensing. I mean, it's worth the commute to come here to do what I'm doing right now, but it is sometimes very lengthy.

Vocational programs are definitely now getting a lot more focus, and schools like ours that are aligned in the industry that has huge need, of course, is creating another major focus for education systems across the country.

The numbers they're predicting, the desire for airlines to find technicians yesterday is already felt, so it's something that we're dealing with. They're putting together packages to try and lure technicians to their company, because the need is so huge.

You can see the world, and you're not locked down at a desk. You're always doing something different. It makes college an option for you instead of a necessity. You know, college isn't the only route to success at aviation, while in other schools, it's pushed, of course.

Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10above the rim and half a million bucks for some of the most electrifying few seconds of basketball. Welcome to Dunk Man. NBA legend Shaquille O'Neal figured, if everybody loves the dunks, why wait for the rest of the game? The first pro league dedicated entirely to competitive dunking.
The best dunkers on the planet came together in Atlanta for the inaugural Dunkman World Championship. With $500,000 on the line, our Andy Scholes was there.

I wanted to bring all the best dunkers, give them their own professional platform. You know, everybody has their internet platform. I wanted to bring these guys, because listen, our professional guys are not stepping up for the fans. I wanted to do something great for the fans.

And the dunks in the final were unbelievable. We saw guys jump over motorcycles, jump over cars. We had a dunker even do the high jump, and in the end, it was 21-year-old high flyer Cam Hazard from Texas that was named the first ever Dunkman World Champion, bringing home a cool half a million dollar prize.

This is my first dunk contest, and I just came out on top. So a lot of people aren't going to believe that, but I just started posting it two years ago. Never thought it would go anywhere, and now I'm on top.

title: Happy World Coconut Day
en: What's up, sunshine? I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10. Happy World Coconut Day.
The coconut might be nature's Swiss army knife. Drink the water, eat the flesh, make milk, oil. Even the husk can be turned into rope, brushes, and other products.
Talk about a fruit that's really cocoa nuts. Ten minutes. Big world. Let's crack into the news.

We start with the end of an era. Lionel Messi, one of the greatest players to ever touch a soccer ball, is retiring from Argentina's national team after more than two decades wearing his country's colors.

The decision follows back-to-back heartbreaks for the soccer superstar. His father, Jorge, passed away shortly after Argentina's loss to Spain in this year's World Cup final. It's a bittersweet moment for fans in Argentina who've watched the homegrown hero rise to the pinnacle of the sport over the years.
There's no comparison. At every level, at a football level, at a personal level, and in the national team, he gave everything. He played the last World Cup 39 years old as if he were a young kid.

He prepared himself as if he were a young kid, knowing what was happening to his father, too. He played it anyway for him. Absolute admiration. He left a lot for Argentina. He went through many periods of ups and downs.

Messi was for me the greatest as a player and as a person, and his retirement makes me sad. But on the other hand, it doesn't displease me because you have to retire at the top, as others did. We're going to miss him because we all love him.
In a statement posted online, Messi thanked Argentine fans for the love they've shown and said he'll miss hearing them cheer from the pitch.
But if you're already missing Messi, don't fret. The 39-year-old Messi will still be playing for defending MLS champions Inter Miami.
Pop quiz hot shot.
How many traditional colours make up the visible light spectrum?
Two, five, seven or ten?

If you said seven, go ahead and celebrate. The human eye perceives different wavelengths on the visible spectrum as the colours red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. Remember the acronym ROYGBIV.

What if we could not only see light, but also hear it? Turns out it's not as far-fetched as it seems, and one innovative creator is taking the seriously bright idea to the next level by making music. Our John Sarlin got a front row seat to hear the unique instrument in action and learn all about the science that makes it work.
Can you guess what triggers this instrument to play music and stops it?
So I made my own instrument that is controlled by light, as you can see here.
You heard that right. This creator has gone viral for using tech and nature to create music.
My name's Riley. I am a composer. I just call it my light instrument.
So how does it work?

These cables basically sense light and how bright it is. That goes into my breadboard that I hand-soldered myself, which then goes into my Arduino, which is right here. That goes into my computer, and I have Arduino code that turns all the stuff that's going into this cable, and it turns it into a bunch of numbers. And then I take all those numbers and I turn it into music.
In other words? Light go into cable. Cable goes into box. Box turns it into electronics. Electronics turns it into sound.
Riley says the idea came about after taking an analog synthesizer building class using similar types of cables.

It sounded awful. It was like, I need to build something kind of like this. That sounds better. I went home, coded, started soldering and building this. And then after four months, I had the instrument.
Since then, Riley says she has performed before mostly academic audiences, as well as posting videos of herself performing with her invention to her social media accounts.
I think it's best live because once it is live, you can actually feel the interaction. You can feel the connection. I like to let the music speak for itself.
Right now, the instrument is limited to the original box and Riley's computer. She says commentators have asked her how to have one to buy, asking donations to help her ongoing artistic project.

I'd love to find a way to make more light instruments because people really want to buy it. People really want to have one of their own. So I'd have to figure out how to make it look nice and how to make it not on a computer. So that's probably like a couple years, maybe some more science and thinking.
Now to Chile, where some of Mother Nature's most dapper dressers are trading their tuxes for something high tech.

My besties, researchers have developed special suits to help injured penguins recover from surgery. Penguins often arrive at rehabilitation centers after getting tangled in fishing nets, suffering wounds that can require stitches. But here's the problem.

Penguins are incredibly flexible, and they can reach around and pick at those stitches. So with prudence, researchers at Chile's Humboldt Conservation Center helped develop a special fabric infused with microscopic particles of copper and zinc, which aid recovery times by preventing bacterial growth and promoting the formation of new blood vessels.
This is a differentiator of this technology versus others, which allows tissues to recover faster.
We're working under the hypothesis that this technology could also help penguin recovery. We have tested it in dogs, cats, mammals, but in penguins for the first time.

And there's a uniquely Chilean twist here. Chile is home to roughly 80 percent of the world's remaining Humboldt penguin population and is the world's largest producer of copper. So one of the country's most famous natural resources is now helping protect some of its most famous wildlife. That's some heavy metal healing right there. Rock on.

Have you ever found yourself crying, like while you're chopping an onion?Imagine doing that in space where tears can float. NASA astronaut Anil Menon shared a look into what cooking might look like hundreds of miles above Earth.
You might even call it one giant leap for a meal prep.
Tell us what's going on here.

We got some onions in a resupply vehicle. We get very excited when we have fruits and vegetables up here. So one of the things that we really like to do is roast these onions. We do it with garlic as well when we get it.
We have some aluminum foil right here and it's very simple. We've got our olive oil. Place the cut onions into the tin foil.

Blasted onion. I like to do a layer of this oil first to help them stick while you're cutting the rest. Get them down there and package it up and then we'll put it over here in our food warmer for probably like 12, 24 hours because it's not a real oven, just a food warmer. But over time that will make a nice roasted onion. They'll even get caramelized as we go for even longer.
