title: Scientists task these “unicorns of the sea” to gather crucial Arctic data
en: Narwhals are moonlighting as climate scientists, a 91-year-old pulled off a jaw-dropping, age-defying feat, and an ambulance powered by sunshine. Rise up, sunshine. I'm Coy Wire, 10 Minutes, Big World, let's get you your news.

We begin in London with some uplifting health news that really is a breath of fresh air. A new study suggests the British capital's efforts to cut vehicle pollution in recent years may be helping children's lungs grow healthier. Researchers focused on the city's ultra-low emission zone, introduced in central London in 2019.

Drivers of vehicles that don't meet strict emission standards have to pay a daily charge, the idea being to put the brakes on tailpipe pollution. The study tracked thousands of kids in London and nearby Luton over several years. Before the clean air zone began, London's kids had higher exposure to traffic pollution and lower average lung function.

But over the four years, between 2018 and 2022, researchers observed a 5% drop in children with clinically impaired lung function in London. In Luton, which didn't have a clean air zone but did make other changes like adding bike paths and lowering speed limits, the rate fell 2%. Researchers say this is the first evidence that clean air zones may actually help child development.

That matters because lungs do most of their growing while we're young. If they don't fully develop by early adulthood, the risk rises later in life for conditions including asthma, emphysema, and chronic bronchitis. So, this isn't just about cleaner air today. It could mean healthier lungs for decades.

Now to Nepal, where nearly a week after catastrophic flooding tore through Himalayan communities, the search for the missing is becoming a race against both time and terrain. As of this taping, more than 1,200 people have died.

Nearly 4,000 are still missing. Relief organizations are helping more than 80,000 residents who've been displaced. The United Nations says some of the hardest hit areas are still unable to even be contacted.

Rescue crews are navigating destroyed roads, unstable mountainsides, while families wait for answers. And in a place where some communities can only be reached from the sky, helicopter crews have become a lifeline. Our Anderson Cooper caught up with one trailblazing pilot helping lead that mission, Nepal's first female helicopter captain, Captain Priya Adhikari.
It's a small place where so many people went missing.
It's extraordinary that you, I mean, the valley is so close and you are flying through this. It's extraordinary.

Just imagine 20 helicopters flying on that valley. Yeah. Continuously talking with each other. That is actually a little bit of pressure to navigate and to radio at the same time and to know who is doing where. And we going to the same place, evacuating from the same place, like five or six helicopters landing. So we need to talk with each other so frequently. Yeah, that is actually.
And now, I mean, you are landing in places where the ground is like liquid cement.
Some of the places you have to be very careful because the helicopter might sink.
It looks from the air, I imagine, to a novice, it looks like, oh, it's solid ground. It's concrete.

No, it's not concrete. This thing that happened, it's bigger than the earthquake we had in 2015. During the earthquake time, it was in different places of Kathmandu or in Nepal. But this is like in a small valley where so many people have lost life. But the smile I have is for the survivors.

I don't know how they survived. Every time I go inland, I see people around. I'm like waving at them and saying like, you survived. You know, the rescues that I'm doing, people lying down inside my helicopter trying to open their eyes. I smile at them and say like, you survived.
Pop quiz, hot shot. A narwhal's famous tusk is made up of what?
Bone, ivory, keratin, or pixie dust.
If you said ivory, you can toot your own horn.
Narwhal tusks are actually overgrown teeth, did you know? And they can grow up to 10 feet long and contain more than 10 million nerve endings.

Narwhals are known as the unicorns of the sea, but scientists are discovering they may make pretty incredible oceanographers. These elusive arctic whales are helping scientists collect data on the crucial ocean currents of a remote and hard-to-study corner of the planet, the rugged coast of East Greenland.

Scientists fitted six narwhals with satellite-transmitting sensors and tracked them for three years as they recorded things like water temperature and salinity in remote Greenland fjords. And the data are helping scientists better understand something called atlantification. That's when warmer, saltier Atlantic water pushes farther into Arctic waters.

And that matters because warmer ocean water can accelerate the melting of glaciers, which then contributes to rising sea levels. Scientists hope this new data will help them better understand the planet's ice sheet.
If anybody tells you you're too old to chase a big dream, let's introduce them to Gray Beard.

Dale Sanders is 91 years old, and he just became the oldest person ever to complete the entire Appalachian Trail. That's roughly 2,200 miles stretching from Georgia all the way to Maine. He began his journey last September and finished atop Maine's highest mountain, Mount Katahdin, on Monday.
This wasn't Sanders' first attempt at the trail. There is a huge, huge difference between hiking the trail at 82 years old and at 91. Huge difference. But it is possible, because I'm proving that.
It is a dangerous hike. Sanders says he fell 71 times. One fall sent him to the hospital. But Gray Beard kept going. I had a chance to learn more about this trail on my own hike. Check this one out.
It kills you physically and you're not sleeping well and you're getting bit by bugs. Ripped open feet. You just keep hiking through it.
Hiking like this for six hours would be a tall task for most, but then there are people who hike this thing for six months. That's just mind-blowing.

You see this white blaze, you know you're on track. That white blaze is the iconic marking of the Appalachian Trail, and it guides hikers along this 2,000-mile contiguous footpath running from Springer Mountain, Georgia to Maine's Mount Katahdin. I've hiked only a tiny sliver of it today, but I want to know more about the trail and the unique individuals like Matt, trail name Road Soda, who dropped everything to conquer it.
You do start to think, like, why am I still doing this? AT hikers spend most nights in tents, but hostels like this allow them to rest up and reconnect.
You have tramilies out here. It's a trail family and usually just forms by the people that are doing the same miles as you a couple nights in a row. That's kind of how you create friends.
I love this man. You don't see him for a couple days, and then when you see him again, it's like you found your long-lost friend again.
You develop bonds through shared adversity that's just, it's pretty incredible.
Thru-hikers suffer through freezing cold, searing heat, rain, wind, loneliness, exhaustion, and lots of pain.
It's a lovely shade of lilac.
My knees have hurt pretty much the entire time.
Three out of four Thru-hikers don't even make it to Maine, but those who push through the pain discover joy, pride, and maybe a new outlook on their planet and fellow humans.
There's this, like, really, really strong community.
Everybody's so on your side all the time.
Every memory resurfaces out here because you just have so much time. And you just look out and just see how beautiful our planet is from a different angle.
There is hope. Four months after we met him, Road Soda and his tramilies finally reached the top of Mount Katahdin. The end of one journey and perhaps the beginning of another.
As rough as this can be, I don't want to leave this life behind.

Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10, an ambulance that runs on sunshine, connecting health care with communities in Kenya. A team of 23 Dutch students called Solar Team Eindhoven tested a prototype solar-powered medical clinic named Stella Juva.

The vehicle carries equipment that can include ultrasound machines, portable x-rays, and other basic diagnostic tools to rural communities far from health facilities and unreliable electricity. The vehicle drove more than 800 kilometers, about 500 miles, through Kenya. The student team says the prototype navigated rough roads and unpaved roads successfully.

So from testing in Kenya, we gathered that Stella Juva is able to handle off-road terrain and being able to drive up to hundreds of kilometers. What we also gathered is that Stella Juva gathers more energy from the sun than it uses with all its medical equipment on board, meaning that we can deliver continuous health care.

The nearly 3,000 pound vehicle was said to be an early demonstration project with more testing ahead, but for communities with a lack of access to health care, this solar-powered ambulance could be a link to a brighter future.
Students looked at a problem. Instead of saying somebody should fix that, they started building something. That is what we call a 10 out of 10.

Hi, Dara. Yeah, this one. That's upside down, but that's me. Thank you guys so much for making us a part of your day.
You made our day. Stay curious, stay kind, shine on, sunshine. I'm Coy Wire and we are CNN 10.

title: Small space, big perks: Inside Paris' historic tiny apartments
en: What's up, Sunshine? Happy Fri-yay! I'm Coy Wire. We've got 10 minutes of news from around the world, so before we get to the weekend, let's finish this week strong. Big questions, big ideas, and tiny little apartments we'll explain later.

We're going to start in New York Citywith a debate sitting right at the intersection of public education and artificial intelligence. Mayor Zoran Mandani is leading the push to ban the use of AI in kindergarten through eighth grades in the nation's largest school district. It's part of a one-year pause on any new proposals.

New York City schools will also disable the AI features in more than 38 previously approved programs that officials say do not meet their new safety and oversight standards. High schoolers will have some access to carefully vetted AI tools under teacher supervision, and they'll be required to learn AI literacy, including how to recognize bias and misinformation and the dangers of overreliance. But mainstream chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude? Off-limits for all grades.
Teachers can still use AI for lesson planning, but not for grading or testing students.
The tech industry wants us to believe that AI in early education is not only inevitable, but that it is necessary. We do not see it that way.

I have yet to see a study showing that AI is beneficial for students in elementary and middle school, with the exception, of course, of research sponsored by the very corporations that stand to profit.

So when does technology help us think and when does it start doing the thinking for us? New York officials say younger students need time to struggle with hard problems, make mistakes and learn alongside human teachers and classmates. In response, some AI companies are rolling out education tools and funding AI training through teachers unions.
New York's policy affects roughly 600,000 younger students and schools around the country will be watching closely.
Women's rights trailblazer and feminist icon Gloria Steinem has died. Steinem's storied career spanned decades.

She became the face of second wave feminism in the 1960s and 70s. She co-founded Ms. magazine and she was also celebrated as an author and journalist. In 2013, then President Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.
Here's Steinem in her own words after receiving that honor.
I feel blessed and enthusiastic and lucky to be part of a movement that is fundamental. Humans are communal animals.

We need to have that kind of shared community which doesn't have to do with how different we are. We need to be different. We learn from difference, not from sameness, but from shared values. And I have that. I mean, that's what you have in a movement. It's huge. And so it enables you to keep going.

A post on her official Instagram page says, quote, Gloria's greatest gift was her ability to listen to others, to make others feel seen and heard. Her words, actions and example gave people permission to be their truest selves.
Pop quiz, hot shot. Which one of these actors did not play or voice Darth Vader in the Star Wars movies?
Jake Lloyd, Hayden Christensen, James Earl Jones or Peter Mayhew?
If you said Peter Mayhew, feel the force. Jake Lloyd, Hayden Christensen and James Earl Jones all portrayed Anakin Skywalker, who went on to become Darth Vader at some point during his life.
Peter Mayhew, he brought Chewbacca to life.

If you've ever wanted to visit a galaxy far, far away, turns out you may only need to go as far as Los Angeles. The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is set to open this month, giving visitors an up-close look at the art behind George Lucas's legendary storytelling universe.
Yes, there is Star Wars with Princess Leia and Obi-Wan. There's also pieces from the entire Lucas archive that would make a Bantha blush. But surprise, this is more than just a Star Wars shrine.
Lucas and his wife, Melody Hobson, created the museum to celebrate something much bigger, the power of pictures to tell stories.
A picture is very powerful and the stories are very powerful. And you combine them together and those two elements create a society.

If podracers and X-Wing fighters aren't your thing, you can still stay on target towards works by iconic artists like Frida Kahlo and Norman Rockwell or famous comic books, pop art and rare concept art from the original Star Wars trilogy.
From Banksy to battle droids, the Lucas Museum is betting that a great story can transcend genres, generations, maybe even galaxies.

Ah, Paris. Home of the Eiffel Tower, countless croissants. But while the City of Light is famous for grand boulevards and beautiful buildings, some Parisians are living in spaces so tiny your bedroom might look like a mansion. Much of central Paris was densely rebuilt during the 1800s, right? With strict rules on building heights.
More than a century later, some of those spaces are still being used as apartments. Our Saskia van Doorn takes us inside some of the French capital's smallest abodes.
These are some of the smallest apartments you'll find in Paris. Some measure less than 100 square feet. A private shower.
Wow. Can you open both doors at the same time? I've never tried, but I guess you could-ish.

They're called chambres de bonnes, maids' rooms, hidden at the top of some of Paris' grandest buildings. Built for domestic servants, they were notoriously cold, with toilets often shared between tenants.
As of 2022, there were still more than 90,000 of these tiny apartments across Paris.

The view from the rooftop is just amazing. You see pretty much every big Parisian monument. My friends commented, oh my gosh, you're going to have a depression in one month's time because it's so tiny, like it's a prison cell. And technically, I guess prison cells are bigger.
Anatoli is an engineering student who's called this place home for the past year. He pays about $800 a month in rent. Expensive by the square foot, but still cheaper than most Parisian apartments.
It's not a sacrifice, it's a trade-off. In engineering, you don't have good solutions, you only have trade-offs. So, yeah.
What's the trade-off here?
The space, or the location, pretty much.
And there's another price to pay for living in central Paris. Lots and lots of stairs.
We do this every day.
It's terrible. I know, it's a sport. Lovely to meet you. Lovely to meet you too. We're going to need a minute.
This is Gladys, and she lives right at the top on the seventh floor.

It's not just Parisians willing to squeeze into these tiny homes. Tourists do it too, paying as much as $140 a night to stay in the heart of Paris. And whether they're here for a night or a year, perhaps this is part of what they're paying for.
Wow. You can see the view. Yes. The Eiffel Tower. Yeah, the Eiffel Tower.
Today's story, getting a 10 out of 10.One man's valiant push to make sure the heroes of September 11th are never forgotten.

As the U.S. will soon mark 25 years since the terrorist attack, retired United Airlines flight attendant Paul Pauli Veneto is pushing an airline beverage cart 220 miles from Boston to Ground Zero in New York City.
The 67-year-old has previously traveled more than 750 miles since launching Pauli's Push in 2021, following routes symbolizing the flight paths of the four hijacked planes.

I made a promise to myself that I would make sure these crew members of these aircrafts were honored and recognized for their heroics. So I went and got four more beverage carts, and I designed each one for each airplane.

Pauli adorned each cart with pictures of the crew members that were lost that day. His journey will take him across 60 cities and towns over a span of 28 days each step, honoring the lives lost on September 11th.
Powerful stuff. All right, no show on Monday in observance of Labor Day, so we're back on Tuesday.

Play that Friday music, Nadir. I'll be on the sidelines for TNT this weekend.
West Virginia hosting Coastal Carolina, so if you see your boy in Morgantown, give me a shout-out. Go and make someone smile this weekend. Remember, you are more powerful than you know.
I'm Coy Wire. This is CNN 10. It's been a blessing to spend this week with you.
